item.title: Semicircle Packing
item.description:
Posts

Semicircle packing

A couple of weeks ago, I entered the GPU World short story competition. I'll post my entry here once the winners are announced. The guidelines imply that I needn't wait until then, but usually writing contests don't allow self-publishing before the end of the competition, so I'd rather not take the risk.

The cash prizes are crazily high for a writing competition: a $40,000 first-place prize; and 7 runner-up prizes of $4,000 each. GPU World's prize pool is 13x to 100x bigger than the other short story competitions I've entered this year.1 If you submit the minimum 1,000 words required and go on to win first place, each word nets you 40 US dollars. It is (well, was) worth a punt.

Alright, enough talk about numbers.

It wasn't until I was halfway through writing my GPU World story that I started to scrutinise where this prize money was coming from. At the bottom of the main contest page, two supporters are listed: Paradigm and Guardian Angel Intelligence Inc. The former, Paradigm is a venture capital firm, which the competition guidelines lists as the provider of the cash prizes. The latter, Guardian Angel Intelligence, piqued my interest with its name alone. I was even more surprised when I clicked on its link and discovered it is an article by Gwern Branwen, who also serves as one of the judges for the competition.2 There is some discussion here on Hacker News about Guardian Angel Intelligence and Gwern's announcement of it, but it is mostly speculative because (at time of writing) there is not much public information about the company itself.

*****

Back to Paradigm. I simultaneously felt two things when I clicked on Paradigm's website:

Awe. Their website is ridiculously cool. To me, it's reminiscent of Ryoji Ikdea.3 Intrigue. Even though I've run a venture-backed startup before, I don't recall hearing about their fund until now.

I spent a few minutes leafing through the flat-futurist interactive visualisations on Paradigm's homepage, and eventually4 found myself on their Puzzles page.

It is at this point I would like to note that I could easily spend my time producing an article about the motivations behind venture capital firms and startups running and funding writing contests. I'm going to earmark this topic for a future essay, as it appears that we are on the precipice of human originality, creativity, and artistic ingenuity being valued far higher than they were just a couple of years ago.

Paradigm's Puzzles page is an eclectic mix of challenges, such as: making a prediction market bot, writing a prompt for an AI agent's negotiation strategy, and Anthropic's original take-home test. Each puzzle has a public leaderboard and you can submit a solution easily by logging in with your X.com account. What I like the most about the puzzles is that they cover the gamut of approachability, in terms of technical ability. While you can try to hand-optimise an Anthropic kernel if you're able to, you could instead write a prompt to pursuade AI buyers that a pen is worth a lot of money.

I spent a bit of time on the persuasion puzzle but since its verifier is closed and rate-limited to 5 tries per hour, it's not the kind of thing I could obsessively try to crack. So, I looked for something else -- ideally something that I could verify locally on my own machine. It was at this point that I stumbled upon the puzzle that took up a great deal of my thinking time thereafter: the one called "Pack Semicircles".

*****

Principally, this semicircle packing puzzle is quite simple. You have to arrange 15 identical semicircles into whatever arrangement you can come up with, with the objective to pack them as tightly together such that when you draw a circle around your arrangement the size of that circle is as small as possible.

With these kinds of experiments, I like to think about things independently first without looking up any kind of answer. There's a tendency these days to just throw the URL of the page at Claude or Codex and have it come up with a solution or explanation (spoiler alert: I do eventually enlist Codex's help), but I want to sautÃ© my own -- likely naÃ¯ve -- approaches before getting external inspiration, at least initially anyway.

I'm a visual thinker and tinkerer, so after sketching in my Remarkable tablet for 15 minutes, I moved over to a graphics editor. I've been mostly using Figma for the past couple of years, but I needed some stronger tooling for dealing with shapes (I used to be a power user of Affinity5 Designer / Photo), so I booted Affinity Photo up first to do some rough arranging.

I started by packing most of the semicircles into a rough "outer fan" shape, with a "core" in the middle that would house the remaining semicircles.

But I realised that the segments for the inner core couldn't just be manually fiddled into place without creating a large, inefficient gap. So I started experimenting (again, manually) with more deliberate symmetry and came up with some pleasing inner packings.

This felt like a great way to work on some visual ideas. It was so much easier using an interactive graphics editor than pen and paper to nucleate different, sometimes random arrangements. But I was still struggling to efficiently pack the shapes together in a way where progress was measurable. Up until now, I had been manually setting the enclosing circle to a radius of 3 -- which would put me in the top â of the leaderboard. Every time I came up with a new visual idea, or tweaked one subset of the semicircles, I had to manually readjust all the other semicircles.

I moved over to Affinity Designer since that has a Symbols6 tool.

Using a mixture of reusable symbol components, and blending modes, I was able to create subgroups of semicircles that I could arrange into different patterns, and automatically repeat and update those patterns as I tweaked them.

I began to realise a couple of things at this point:

Getting an efficient packing of the semicircles with a symmetrical layout is very fiddly -- even in graphics software that has tools for reusable symbols. In isolation, I was discovering asymmetrical tweaks which allowed me to pack certain groupings more efficiently. This was also very fiddly.

I realised that I wanted to build my own visualisation tool. But since I was coming to the end of my initial independent research on this problem, I decided to see what research existed out there just in case that would help inform any tool I decided to build for myself.

Surprisingly, there really isn't much on the internet about efficient arrangements of semicircles! Maybe that isn't so surprising to other people, but I was having a lot of fun doing this, and there is a tonne of work on the internet about regular circle packing, or shape packing in general. I assume the author of the Paradigm shape packing puzzle intentionally chose an odd number of semicircles, because otherwise an even number of semicircles could just be combined into circles and therefore benefit from the wealth of circle packing research out there.7

I found one blogspot (remember blogspot?) post about semicircle packing. The author laments the lack of existing research on semicircle packing and cites one Math Exchange post -- which also ironically laments the lack of existing literature. I was excited about discovering this post, but it ended up being somewhat of a dead-end for me, especially since the author seems to be talking more about even numbers of semicircles.

So I set out to create a piece of software that would allow me to quickly visualise symmetrical semicircle layouts, which solved the two problems (or realisations) I had when using graphics software manually: easy creation of symmetrical layouts, and asymmetrical tweaks to these layouts.

After some back and forth with Codex, I landed somewhere promising with just a couple hours' development time.

You can try it at puzzles.rorz.io/semicircle-packing.

I got exactly what I wanted: a tool that let me arrange as many layers of fanned semicircles (i.e. equally spaced, angled, and oriented) as I wished. Once I'd had fun creating trivial layouts of symmetrical fans manually, I added a new mode called Tighten which would adjust each fan layer's settings to most optimally pack them together into a smallest-as-possible radius.

Just as with my experiments in Affinity Designer, after a while Codex came to the same conclusion as me: we needed a way to make asymmetric tweaks to the overall layout in order to more efficiently pack the semicircles further. The purist in me wanted the best solution to be symmetrical, but the leaderboard containing many results below my symmetrical best of 2.97 had me thinking that this was a futile ideal to pursue.

As a result, a Relax mode was introduced which splits each fan layout into individual layers. These are then tweaked by a search algorithm in order to keep bringing down the enclosing radius as much as possible.

I got to about 2.96 using my tool alone, but that still only had me in the top 50% of the leaderboard. I realised at this point that I needed help from Codex.

I spent a chunk of my weekly Codex usage on Astra Max and Ultra, as well as Sol Ultra and Terra Ultra -- all of which managed to find different approaches using the UI that I'd built up until now. Dynomight's notes on "doing math" were useful reading at this point in order to develop strategies that would get more juice out of Codex's models. Eventually, after getting to the top-10 in the leaderboard and stalling, I decided to take a fresh approach and fork the original Python repo.

After hill-climbing different solutions, I managed to get into the top 3 on the leaderboard (where I've since stayed) with a radius of 2.94853.

Here's the visualisation of that submission:

It's not symmetrical at all!8

While I was in the process of hill-climbing a better solution, Astra Ultra came across a PDF of a paper that the #1 position on the leaderboard entrant (and their agent) created, detailing the various strategies they tried. Sadly, none of these were able to help me and Codex beat them.

*****

Something I reflect on after having spent a few days tinkering with this is that I got the most dopamine from getting Bronze on the leaderboard by way of brute-forcing with Codex; but I got the most fulfilment from sketching out the shapes in my graphics editor and working with Codex to build a custom visualisation tool. I had a tonne of fun working on this problem, and will keep chipping away at it in Codex. I'm also going to update puzzles.rorz.io with more tools as and when I get round to it.

Footnotes

I entered two short story competitions in the UK this year. One had a prize pool of Â£7,500, the other Â£1,000. GPU World's prize pool is $100,000. â©

It is fun to see that it's the same Gwern (of Gwern.net fame) who I used to read a lot of when I was at university. Gwern was also recently a judge on the 1Picture1000Words competition which I published my entry for here. â©

I've been to many Ryoji Ikeda exhibitions in London, and I would say that he is probably my favourite artist. I recently made the hero image on my LinkedIn profile a pastiche of Ikeda's datamatics work. You can play around with my implementation and view its code here. â©

Note to maintainers of Paradigm's website: It's quite hard to spot the link to the Puzzles page as your homepage currently points to https://www.paradigm.xyz/research#paradigm-puzzles from its navigation menu instead of /puzzles. â©

Affinity has since discontinued these individual desktop apps after being acquired by Canva. â©

I couldn't find a relevant resource to link to here -- the latest documentation is for the superseded version. â©

That is to say that breaking up circles into semicircles may still yield much more efficient packings. â©

It does have some interesting properties though, and pseudo-symmetry. Perhaps more detail for a later post. â©

item.title: PyPI's redesigned project pages with clearer security signals are now live
item.description:
PyPI's redesigned project pages with clearer security signals are now live

In July, we announced a series of planned updates to the PyPI user interface. Shaped by user research with members of the Python community, the updates aim to improve how we surface security signals and display package details.

We're pleased to share that this work is now complete and live on PyPI.

Context¶

With the rapid growth of the Python ecosystem, PyPI has become an increasingly attractive target for malicious actors. In response, the PyPI team has delivered many security features while taking a more active role in helping PyPI users assess and understand package security.

Digital attestations, introduced in 2024, are an example of this effort, providing a verifiable record of a release file's provenance (where it came from). However, provenance and attestations are still unfamiliar concepts for many PyPI users, and PyPI's interface did little to communicate their meaning, importance, or limitations.

To address this, PyPI partnered with Kabu Creative to bring clearer security signals to the PyPI UI, implementing the recommendations developed in the OpenSSF Attestations Style Guide.

Here's a look at what's changed, what it means for you, and what actions you can take.

The New Security Tab¶

The new security tab communicates release provenance states and displays per-file attestations, giving you a dedicated place to verify where the release files came from.

Provenance States¶

PyPI calculates each release's provenance state by checking whether each release file has an attestation. Typically, a release will be in one of two states:

Full Provenance¶

This means that 100% of the release files have attestations, carrying either or both of the supported attestation types:

PyPI Publish attestations confirm the file was published by a PyPI Trusted Publisher:

SLSA Build Provenance attestations link the file back to its exact source commit, build platform, and instructions:

You can review attestation metadata directly in the UI, or click on the transparency log link for more information.

No Provenance¶

"No provenance" simply means that no file in the release has an attestation. This is typical for older releases or projects that have not yet configured Trusted Publishing. No provenance does not necessarily indicate that a release or release file is malicious; it instead means that the file origin cannot be cryptographically verified.

When there is no provenance, you should rely on surrounding trust signals to assess security, such as maintainer history, release patterns, and repository activity. If you maintain the package, consider using Trusted Publishing with a publisher that generates attestations for your next release.

Provenance Warnings¶

Provenance warnings are designed to help you identify when a file may not have come from the project's maintainers, for example, if an attacker has taken over an account or a publishing workflow.

When provenance metadata looks unusual or conflicts with a project's history, PyPI surfaces a prominent warning. Many warnings have legitimate explanations, but each one is worth checking before you install.

Incomplete Provenance¶

This means that some files carry attestations while others do not (e.g., wheels were published via Trusted Publishing, but the source tarball was uploaded using an API token).

Exercise caution if you see this warning. Check release notes for build issues or ask in the project's issue tracker before installing.

Inconsistent Provenance¶

This warning indicates that files within the same release originate from different build systems or source repositories.

Check the attestation metadata to confirm whether all files came from sources controlled by the maintainers.

Change of Provenance¶

This warning tells you that the release files originated from a different repository or workflow than a previous release. While often legitimate (such as an organization name change or repository migration), it can also indicate a compromised pipeline or account takeover.

If you see this warning, check the project release notes or official channels to confirm that an infrastructure migration was planned.

Loss of Provenance¶

This means that a project that previously published with attestations has changed to uploading release files without them.

Check whether the maintainers intentionally changed their publishing process, for example by switching back to API tokens, or by changing their publishing configuration so that it no longer generates attestations. If this is unexpected, treat the release with skepticism until verified.

To learn more about provenance and attestations, including provenance warnings, see our user documentation.

Redesigned Project Detail Page¶

To support these changes, the project detail page has also been updated:

Provenance warnings now appear at the top of the page, alongside status banners for yanked releases, archived projects, and pre-releases. If a project or release is quarantined, only the quarantine banner is shown, as it takes precedence over all other warnings and banners. When a release has full provenance or provenance warnings, its provenance state is displayed in the sidebar, linking through to the security tab for more information. Metadata is now ordered by utility and labeled as "PyPI data" or "Data verified by PyPI", replacing the old design where data was grouped and ordered by verification status. Release Files and Release History¶

The redesigned release files tab helps you find the right file by searching and filtering long lists. You can also view the provenance state of each file within the table, and quickly identify late files, which are marked with an orange warning icon.

Late file warnings are shown when one or more files were uploaded more than 14 days after the initial release timestamp. These warnings only appear on releases prior to July 2026, when a policy was introduced to reject new files after 14 days.

The release history tab now also provides more details about each release, exposing file count, provenance state, and release status (i.e., quarantined, yanked, archived, or pre-release).

Getting Help¶

Alongside the interface updates, PyPI's user documentation has been extended to help you better navigate package security. Read our package security guide to learn about:

Looking Ahead & Acknowledgments¶

The new security tab gives PyPI a dedicated home for future attestation types and security notices. To help the wider open source ecosystem benefit from this work, we've also published a case study in the OpenSSF Attestations Style Guide detailing the design patterns and warnings developed during this project.

This initiative was funded by the Open Source Security Foundation and implemented by Kabu Creative. We would like to thank Dustin Ingram, Zach Steindler, and the members of the OpenSSF Securing Software Repositories Working Group for championing this effort. Special thanks to Mike Fiedler, Jacob Coffee, and members of the PyPI team for their thoughtful design feedback and code reviews, @cofiem for their contributions to the new release files tab, and our user interview participants and community testers for helping shape the final design.

Finally, we would like to thank the OpenSSF for its funding and continued partnership in securing the Python packaging ecosystem.

item.title: Lovable apps expose passport details and more than 200K private messages
item.description:
Lovable: Many Apps Built on the Platform Expose Sensitive Data

AI makes it easier to build your own web applications, but handling sensitive data still requires special care. We examined 159,041 Lovable projects and found many cases where personal and confidential information was accessible without logging in.

About Lovable

Lovable is a Swedish AI startup founded in Stockholm in 2023 by Anton Osika and Fabian Hedin. The platform turns plain-language descriptions into web applications and is designed to be accessible even to people with little or no programming experience.

Lovable grew out of Osika’s open-source project “GPT Engineer”, released in 2023. The project evolved into the GPT Engineer App before being renamed Lovable in late 2024 and launching publicly that November.

The Promise

Lovable can build impressively sophisticated web projects with AI, from static websites to full applications with user management and database connections. But as soon as an application handles confidential information, one question becomes crucial: Is that data protected against unauthorized access?

In its marketing, Lovable repeatedly emphasizes that no technical knowledge is needed to build projects. This can give the impression that the platform takes care of security too. Yet Lovable’s Terms & Conditions place responsibility for applications and data handling on the customers themselves.

That leaves a troubling gap between the promise of an easy-to-use, all-in-one service and the responsibilities customers are expected to take on.

Against this backdrop, we investigated how well sensitive data in Lovable applications is protected, in collaboration with Handelsblatt. Lina Knees reported on the findings on November 2, 2026 (in German).

Research Question

We wanted to find out whether sensitive data in Lovable applications was accessible without logging in. We looked separately at data sent when a website first loaded and additional content we checked by making further read-only requests with the same API key.

The result: We found many clear examples of sensitive data left unprotected.

Methodology

We focused on the database service Supabase. Its integration is relatively easy to analyze, and we believe it is the most widely used database service among Lovable projects. Lovable’s own database features, introduced in late 2025, are still less widely used. Similar misconfigurations may occur there too, but we did not examine them in this analysis.

Using datasets from the open web archive Common Crawl, we identified and analyzed 159,041 Lovable projects from December 2025 to September 2026. Of these, 34,545 used Supabase.

24,664 websites sent database records from Supabase as soon as they loaded, without requiring a login or any other interaction. That alone is not a security issue: the data may be intended for public display. But by making additional read-only requests, we were able to retrieve more database content. We found records containing email addresses in 10,560 tables across 7,403 of the 24,664 websites (30%).

Limitations

Email addresses can help identify records containing personal data, but they may also be public contact addresses or test data. At the same time, this approach misses personal records that contain no email address. These effects partly offset one another, though we could not establish to what extent. The 30% figure should therefore not be read as a confirmed data leak rate. It applies only to the 24,664 websites we examined more closely. Our sample, drawn from Common Crawl, is also not representative of all Lovable applications.

We retrieved only parts of the datasets rather than downloading them in full. The figures below reflect the records we actually downloaded; the affected datasets may contain more. We are not publishing details of how to access them, as doing so could make further access easier.

Data Leaks

We found many serious cases of exposed data, including:

A German lifestyle forum exposed more than 80,000 profiles containing full names, email addresses, dates of birth, and gender information. More than 200,000 chat messages were also accessible.

Several event organizers and restaurants exposed tens of thousands of records relating to ticket and food sales, with no login required. The records we inspected included email addresses, phone numbers, postal addresses, payment information, and ticket codes.

A property management company exposed AI-generated summaries of internal emails containing sensitive information about tenants, property owners, and business partners.

In a particularly serious case, a service provider exposed more than 1,000 records containing identity document details, including passport numbers, expiration dates, and nationalities. These highly sensitive identity details could be used for identity theft.

Other accessible content included tens of thousands of contracts, invoices, personal photo albums, and internal WhatsApp communications.

We also found numerous newsletter subscriptions, waiting lists, and contact and support inquiries. In one case, 280,000 emails sent to a provider’s customers were accessible.

Depending on what it contains, exposed data like this could be used for phishing, ticket fraud, or identity theft. We could not establish whether any of it had been misused.

Handelsblatt contacted Lovable with the findings of our investigation.

Implications

Our analysis shows that many Lovable applications leave even highly sensitive data unprotected, with potentially serious consequences for the people affected.

Access control mistakes can happen in any application, whether written by people or built with AI. With Lovable, database integrations follow recurring patterns, making it easier for attackers to look for similar misconfigurations across many applications. An approach that works against one app may then work against others with little extra effort. Users without a technical background also face a harder task spotting and preventing these flaws.

An easy-to-use development platform does not remove the need for an expert review of access permissions before an application handles confidential data.

Automated checks are no substitute for a professional security assessment.

Before an application handles real customer or business data, its access permissions, interfaces, and separation between user accounts should be reviewed. These checks should be repeated after significant changes. If the necessary expertise is not available in-house, bring in qualified support.

If you would like help securing your application, please get in touch.

Note: This research report presents a more recent analysis and updated figures compared with the Handelsblatt article published on November 2, 2026.

item.title: A family tree of software job titles
item.description:
For a few years I was ‘Head of DevOps’. Before I got that job title I’d done much the same work under other names, and since then I’ve watched the same work get called SRE, and then it seemed to morph towards platform engineering. If you’ve been in this industry for any length of time you’ll have seen titles come and go like this, and you might have wondered where they all came from.

So I (with the help of Mr Claude) built this family tree of software job titles, from the 1940s to now.

It’s here: ianmiell.github.io/sw-job-title-family-tree

What It Is

There are 104 titles, from ‘Computer’ (a person, not a machine) at the top to ‘AI Agent / Context Engineer’ at the bottom.

Time runs from top to bottom, in five-year rows. The titles sit in seven coloured columns by family:

Development Analysis, architecture and leadership Operations and infrastructure Networks and security Data and AI Quality and test Support and customer-facing

A solid arrow means the title grew out of its parent. A dashed arrow means influence, or a common career move. Landmark titles are in bold.

On the site you can click a family to see just that column (here’s Data & AI), or click a title to get its history, background and connections (here’s SRE).

The whole thing is one Graphviz file and one JSON file of descriptions. Each title is one line in the .dot file, and the picture is rendered with:

$ dot -Tsvg job_title_family_tree.dot -o job_title_family_tree.svg

Adding a title is three small edits: a node in its family’s column, an entry in the row for its five-year period, and its parent arrows.

A word on the dates. They’re roughly when a title became common, not its first recorded use, and they’re my best estimates, not sourced citations. Some are well known (SRE at Google in 2003, ‘DevOps’ coined in 2009, ‘Data Scientist’ in 2008). Plenty are a ‘c.’ and a shrug.

Six Things I Noticed

Drawing it out made a few patterns hard to miss.

1) Coding Started Out as the Clerical Bit

In 1947, Goldstine and von Neumann’s ‘Planning and Coding of Problems’ split the work of using a computer in two: mathematicians planned the problem, and coders translated the plan into machine instructions. Coding was treated as lower-status clerical work, and much of it was done by women.

It turned out that coding eventually became the hard, creative part, and the coder merged into the programmer.

Go back further and it’s stranger still. Several of the first ENIAC programmers were recruited from the Army’s human computers, people whose job was to compute by hand. So the job gave its name to the machine, and its people to programming.

My upcoming book, available in Early Release with O’Reilly.

2) Titles Break Apart, Then Join Back Up

The webmaster turned up around 1993, and was often a single person who wrote the HTML, ran the webserver (often a box under a desk), answered the email, and kept the site up (sometimes by kicking it, more often by plugging it back in after kicking it).

By the mid-2000s the title had all but gone, as it was unfashionably ancient. The code went to web developers, the servers to sysadmins, and the content to editors and designers.

Then the web developer split into front-end and back-end around 2005, and the two joined back up again as ‘full-stack’ around 2008.

This is the centralisation/distribution see-saw I’ve written about before, playing out in job titles.

3) Some Titles Don’t Last

The prompt engineer made headlines in 2023 with a few eye-wateringly well-paid job listings. As the models got better, the skill became part of other jobs, and on the tree it gets absorbed into the AI engineer almost as soon as it appears.

The scrum master is a slower version of the same story: demand peaked in the 2010s, and many organisations have since folded it back into engineering management or delivery roles.

The newest title on the tree is the ‘AI Agent / Context Engineer’ (c. 2025). The description for it currently says “time will tell whether it stays a separate title”. I’m not taking bets.

4) Names Get Recycled

‘Systems Engineer’ is two different jobs on the tree. At IBM in the 1960s it was a pre-sales role, working with customers to design installations and get them running. In the 1990s, thanks largely to Microsoft’s MCSE certification, it meant a more senior, design-oriented sysadmin. Same title, different branch, no relation.

‘Configuration management’ started as a 1960s US defence discipline for tracking hardware changes, became software version control in the 1970s, and then came back decades later as the name for tools like Puppet and Chef.

5) The New Thing Is Often an Old Thing

The ‘forward deployed engineer’ (FDE) is one of the hottest titles of 2025, as OpenAI, Anthropic and plenty of AI startups hire FDEs to get AI working inside their customers’ organisations.

Palantir built its business around them from about 2010: software engineers embedded with a customer, often on site, building whatever is needed to make the product work for that customer’s problem.

Which sounds a lot like IBM’s systems engineers of the 1960s, who worked with customers before and after the sale, designing installations and getting systems running. (It also sounds a lot like old-style consulting, but I would say that.)

6) The DevOps Debate Is There

Ben Treynor Sloss defined SRE as “what happens when you ask a software engineer to design an operations team”. DevOps was meant as a culture of developers and operations working together, but by about 2011 ‘DevOps Engineer’ had become a job title, usually for whoever did the automation. On the tree, the arrow between SRE and DevOps points both ways. Platform engineering has both of them as parents, and was sold around 2022 as ‘the successor to DevOps’.

The Dev/Ops divide has never been resolved. It just keeps getting new names.

Why Bother?

When I’m asked what the difference is between a DevOps engineer, an SRE and a platform engineer, the honest answer is always a little history lesson. This is the shortest version of that lesson I’ve managed so far.

The dates are best guesses, and I’ll have missed titles, mangled some lineages and drawn arrows people will argue with. If you know better, let me know, or raise a PR on the repo.

Which brings me back to the coders.

In 1947 coding was the clerical bit, and the real work was in the planning. Wind forward eighty years and you’ll hear much the same said about coding again, because AI. Last time, the coders turned out to be doing the hard part.

I’ll leave you to draw that arrow yourself.

item.description:
How the Telephone Changed the World James Gleick Explores the Technological and Cultural Impact of an Invention That Transformed Civilization

A beige plastic telephone sits on a wooden table. The handset, attached by a coiled cord, rests in its cradle. The base has a clear dial with ten finger holes. The telephone is the most ordinary of household objects but, sitting silently on the table, it seems to portend something. It’s bound to ring.

Suddenly it does: a metallic brrrrring, distinctive and familiar. Nearby on the carpet, a smiling girl with pigtails and a ruffled-sleeve dress leaps to her feet, races over, and picks up the handset. She holds a stuffed toy duck to the receiver. Quack! Quack! Quack!

“That’s no way to answer the phone, Susie!” says an older boy, appearing in the frame. He has neatly brushed brown hair and wears a white shirt buttoned to the neck. He grabs the handset from Susie and demonstrates proper etiquette: “Hello. Matthews residence. This is Jimmy.” He listens and speaks again. “Just a minute, please.”

A grown-up arrives, smiling, also wearing his hair neatly parted, with a button-down shirt and khaki trousers. “Uncle Bill,” Jimmy tells him earnestly, “Captain Adams wants to talk to you.”

“Thanks, Jimmy,” says Bill. He takes the handset and holds it to his ear, stretching its coiled cord. “Hi, Captain, this is Bill,” he says. “No, we don’t usually have ducks answer the phone. That one belongs to Susie.” No time for jokes, though. Captain Adams needs Uncle Bill to come at once. These are the whitest white people you’ve ever seen, performing a fantasy of middle-class American life familiar from TV sitcoms that featured Wally and Beaver, Mike and Robbie and Chip.

Eighty-nine years into the telephone era, this wholesome scene opened a movie called We Learn About the Telephone, made in Technicolor on behalf of American Telephone and Telegraph (AT&T) by a well-known Hollywood producer, Jerry Fairbanks. The film was distributed as a public service to schools around the country and played for a captive audience of children in classrooms. In 1965, the United States had one telephone for every four people; the number had tripled in the two decades since World War II. It already seemed the universal appliance. Yet the phone company—there was basically just one—still thought its customers needed instruction.

Back to the show. Little Jimmy asks: “What did people do before the telephone was invented? How’d they get messages to each other in a hurry?”

The paradox of the telephone was its plainness, its tendency to hide in the background while changing everything around it.

Thus prompted, Uncle Bill draws a cartoon character called Mister Man, who begins to speak. (If his voice sounds familiar, it’s because AT&T hired the best: Mel Blanc, the onetime vaudevillian who voiced Bugs Bunny, Daffy Duck, and many other characters.) Mister Man guides us through a potted history of human communication, beginning with the “cave men” and the Egyptians. “The only way Mr. Caveman knew how to get a message from one place to another was to send a runner,” Bill explains. Greeks used runners, too, and Romans, until they discovered horses. Then came knights and cowboys. “That’s a Pony Express rider!” says Jimmy. “That’s right,” Bill replies. “But man wanted to send messages faster than a runner or a horse could travel.” A cartoon Indian sends smoke signals. Sailors communicate from ship to ship with flashing mirrors and blinking lights. Then the telegraph appears. “Man has always been able to solve his problems by inventing new things…The telegraph was, and still is, wonderful,” Uncle Bill explains. But the telegraph was not enough. “Mister Man wanted to send his voice over a distance, to carry on a real conversation,” Uncle Bill continues. “Then in 1876 a man named Alexander Graham Bell found a way. He invented the telephone.”

This was the story in a nutshell. It was not entirely true, but it served as the essential origin story of its sponsor, the greatest commercial enterprise the world had ever known. AT&T, known as the Bell System, held more capital and generated more income than most nation-states. Its scientific research arm, the Bell Telephone Laboratories, was unique in the world, eventually the source of eleven Nobel Prizes in physics and chemistry. Mister Man was right to place the telephone at the head of a line of increasingly powerful information technologies. Humanity had learned to send its voice—its many voices—disembodied, far and wide, eliminating walls, bridging towns and countryside, inviting conversation with strangers unseen.

No single genius accomplished that, and it didn’t happen all at once. No one had felt the absence of telephones before they existed, and at first hardly anyone understood what they might be good for. Much that seems obvious in retrospect had to be learned by people feeling their way toward the future.

*

AT&T had no trouble inserting its potted history into the curriculum of millions of primary-school children, and after the history lesson came some instruction in how to use the device. It was hardly necessary. Most people had a telephone at home that looked exactly like the one in the movie. The Western Electric model 500 was ubiquitous across the United States. It first appeared in 1949 and hardly changed as the years passed: a thermoplastic shell screwed to a metal base, a clear plastic finger wheel, and a handset with a mouthpiece and an ear-piece attached by a cord twisted in a stiff spiral. The phone was heavy, about four pounds, but a person could pick it up with two fingers under the cradle while nestling the handset between shoulder and neck. That was actually comfortable, when people got used to it. If they opened the base by turning it over and removing some screws, they could see a pair of brass bells, with a small clapper between them, and a few colored wires. Ordinary as it was, it spoke of modernity, with its sculpted plastic. No other household gadget had anything like that dial.

When the telephone rang, it did not chirp or chime or play a tune; it just rang. The sound was the same throughout the United States and much of the world: an electromechanical bell ringing for two seconds at a time, with a four-second pause in between. (Older people will never forget that sound, and it can still be heard in old movies and television shows. Nostalgists have been known to install “Old Telephone” as the ringtone for their smartphone.)

At first the telephones were all black; then AT&T customers could choose among ivory, gray, beige, and a few more colors. The phones remained simple, undramatic, and unadorned. Yet they ripped invisible tunnels through space—like wormholes, only real.

More than eight in ten homes in the United States had a Bell System telephone—owned by the company, merely on loan to the customer. No other company was allowed to manufacture telephones, and everyone’s telephones were the same. People thought that was a normal state of affairs: it had always been like that and it always would be.

The phone was a simple object with not so much as an on-off switch, but the Bell System never stopped educating the public in its proper use. Uncle Bill and Mister Man offered children some dos and don’ts. Don’t shout into the telephone. Do use your normal speaking voice. Speak directly into the mouthpiece. It’s important to speak clearly. Don’t let the phone ring too long before answering—“but if you’re the person making the call, you should let the phone ring eight to ten times.”

There is even a lesson in dialing, using the finger wheel to choose the desired telephone number: “When you dial, you should make sure you bring your finger all the way around to the finger stop. Then for each number let the dial go all the way back by itself. Each number. All the way. Then let go. See?”

Everyone knew how to dial the phone. It was no harder than, for example, learning to tie one’s shoelaces. But the Bell System left little to chance. It was relentless. Far more than outsiders knew, it had made itself the author of its own story. The company subsidized books by supposedly independent authors; it sponsored articles, speeches, and pamphlets; and it arranged lectures for business schools and law schools on such matters as public-utility regulation. The slick Jerry Fairbanks movie was one of many instructional films and cartoons. Schoolteachers received a twenty-four-page booklet, also titled We Learn About the Telephone, full of helpful material. A section called “The Telephone Brings Everybody Together” listed, with illustrations, some of the people you can call: the repairman, storekeepers, the fireman, the policeman, and the doctor.

Half a century earlier, the Bell System advertised itself as “The Sign Board of Civilization.” Its full name was the American Telephone and Telegraph Company and Associated Companies. Its logo was a great bell, deliberately resembling the Liberty Bell, bearing the words “Local and Long Distance Telephone.” Advertisements in magazines and newspapers said:

Wherever you see this sign, it stands for civilization. It is the sign of one of the most powerful influences for broadening human intelligence…

Bell telephone service has brought the entire country up to the same instant of progress.

It has unified the Nation…

You can see this march of progress right in your own neighborhood. Every little while some neighbor has a Bell telephone put in. If you have one, every new subscriber enlarges the scope of your personal contact.

The copywriters could not resist adding a threat: “If you have not, every new telephone makes you the more isolated.” This was the essence of the company’s business model: every new subscriber adds value for every other.

*

Children in 1965 were growing up in a world transformed, normal though it seemed to them. Everyone had from birth at least a vague awareness of an invisible web of voices, bringing the unreachable within reach. It was already hard to remember the earlier world, where the loudest shout would barely carry to the next room. The paradox of the telephone was its plainness, its tendency to hide in the background while changing everything around it. When the telephone was still new, Marcel Proust in France saw it already growing old and familiar, “a supernatural instrument before whose miracles we used to stand amazed, and which we now employ without giving it a thought, to summon our tailor or order an ice cream.”

By 1965, teaching children how to dial the telephone was unnecessary. But in the next century the knowledge would be lost again, and YouTube would feature videos of youngsters baffled by ancient rotary telephones. “This is like phones that my mom used as a kid?” “How does this even work?” “It looks like a phone, it has a telephone and it has numbers.”

The telephone had other inventors besides Alexander Graham Bell, an amateur who did not know much about electricity. Neither the idea nor the device came to any one person in a visionary flash. Even with the new invention in hand, the most expert entrepreneurs and government officials had trouble seeing what it was for. The president of the Western Union Telegraph Company dismissed it. “What use could this company make of an electrical toy?” he said, thus condemning his business to stagnation and decline. We might say the telephone was invented by the people who used it. They made it what it is, creating new habits and a new language as they went. Or we might say the telephone invented itself: it was an inevitability; it had to come, and when it came it could not be stopped, an invasive species dragging its wires through cracks in the familiar world.

We have learned by now that gadgets can have a life of their own and an influence we cannot evade. Using a technology changes a person. Using a technology changes a culture.

First the telephone was a curiosity, then a luxury item, and then an ordinary necessity. In 1965, people made something like 100 billion telephone calls a year, long and short, local and long-distance; that number has increased a thousand-fold, but even then the telephone had helped humanity coalesce into a wired collective—trading news and rumors, mingling public intelligence with private gossip. The telephone company could help its customers learn about the telephone, but it could hardly explain the changes that four-pound box of plastic and metal had already worked in the fabric of modern life and in the psyches of the people who put their ears and mouths to it.

The telephone enabled the expansion of cities and the creation of suburbs by freeing workspaces and living spaces from the requirement of proximity. It encouraged nationhood by softening the differences between regions. “The service of the telephone in the consolidation of our Union was an epoch-making service,” wrote Michael Pupin at Columbia University in 1930. “No other country availed itself of the consolidating power of the telephone as much as this country did. No other country needed it so much.”

The telephone brought a generation of women into the workforce for the first time. The job of telephone operator—a profession like none that had ever existed—required intelligence, physical dexterity, mental focus, and genial patience, and it was decided by universal consent that the job belonged to women.

The telephone marked the beginning of a rebalancing of the senses in human culture: it re-centered sound and hearing, which had been deprecated during the long rise of text as the mode of communication most reliable, most stable, most respected. “As there was an Enlightenment, so too was there an ‘Ensoniment,’” argues Jonathan Sterne, a scholar of media and culture. That rebalancing continues.

Was it a connector, a unifier? Or a disrupter of precious solitude? Sociologists argued about what the telephone had done to shape the evolution of modern culture, to alter social habits and relationships. They even argued about whether it could have done anything—whether any technology in itself could dictate human affairs. Some doubted that. People made the telephone, some said; people decided how to use it, so let’s not fall into the trap of granting it agency. The violin doesn’t play the violinist. “No single invention—and no group of them taken together in isolation from nontechnological elements—ever changed the direction in which a society was going,” George Daniels wrote in 1970. “Habits seem to grow out of other habits far more directly than they do out of gadgets.”

But we have learned by now that gadgets can have a life of their own and an influence we cannot evade. Using a technology changes a person. Using a technology changes a culture.

After the telegraph laid the groundwork, establishing the possibility of nearly instantaneous long-distance communication across networks of wires, the telephone became the first piece of what later coalesced into the phenomenon called mass media—the incessant, ubiquitous exchange of information conducted point-to-point via telephones and telefaxes, broadcast via radio and television, and stored and shared as phonographs, photographs, and cinema. Media, distinct from mechanism, required theorists, such as Marshall McLuhan, who asserted its primacy with his clever slogan “The medium is the message.”

The telephone became a cultural artifact and a generator of other artifacts. The ability to speak across space transformed business organizations, military tactics, the rules of etiquette, the rituals of romance. Each profession evolved in its own way, from news gathering to sex work. (“The prostitute was a specialist, and the call-girl is not,” McLuhan declared coolly in 1965.) Other powerful technologies arose alongside the telephone and followed after, but the telephone was special. It conferred upon every individual a power to communicate that was essential in the development of modern life.

It left a trail of appurtenances: the party line, the busy signal, the dial tone, the collect call, the wiretap, the answering machine, the telephone book, the telephone booth. Telephone booths, boxes, kiosks, and cabins, varying from country to country, appeared on public sidewalks; these structures had no other purpose but to house telephones and shelter their users. Anyone old enough to remember telephone booths retains a mental image of a characteristic design—in Britain, a cast-iron box, usually painted red, with a rounded roof, a single door, two mullioned windows, and a classical pediment bearing the royal crest. Some urban children imagined that pay phones whisked their coins through underground pipes to a central repository. Besides allowing people to make calls in semi-privacy, telephone booths spun off oddities of their own. In the mid-twentieth century, pranksters competed to see how many people could squeeze into a telephone booth at once. The comic-book hero Superman used telephone booths to shed his civilian garb; this became so familiar a trope that it inspired a sight gag in the 1978 movie Superman in which Clark Kent dashed for a phone booth and was dismayed to find its modern replacement, a pay phone mounted on a post. Special heroes required special phones: Dick Tracy a wrist radio, Batman his Bat Phone, and Maxwell Smart his shoe phone. Star Trek’s spacefarers had flip phones (“communicators”) twenty years before such things appeared in real life. Meanwhile, the science-fiction paladin Doctor Who traveled through space and time in a vehicle that took the form of the British telephone box. It was bigger on the inside than it appeared from the outside. All phone booths were.

And then, in an eye blink, the phone booths were left to rust, the phone books stopped arriving at the door, and the busy signal and the party line and all the rest became memories. The telephone turned into something else entirely.

______________________________

From The Telephone: A New History by James Gleick. Copyright © 2026. Published by Farrar, Straus and Giroux, a division of Macmillan.

James Gleick

James Gleick is a historian and biographer whose books include The Information, winner of the Royal Society and PEN/America science-writing prizes, and Chaos, a Pulitzer Prize and National Book Award finalist. They have been translated into thirty languages. He lives in New York and London.

item.title: Court denies motion to dismiss DRAM price fixing case
item.description:
Key Points Judge Noël Wise denied in full Samsung, SK Hynix and Micron's joint motion to dismiss a proposed class action alleging they conspired to cut supply of conventional DRAM, such as DDR5, and shift capacity to HBM. The court held the case was not a rerun of DRAM II, the Ninth Circuit's 2022 affirmance of dismissal of an earlier DRAM conspiracy suit against the same companies. The judge found that long-term HBM lock-ups, refusals of long-term conventional DRAM contracts, Micron's Crucial closure, fab delays, the failure to expand despite record prices, near-identical customer vetting and the companies' prior cartel history supported a plausible inference of conspiracy. The court gave no weight to three of the plaintiffs' arguments: investor statements about "supply discipline," which it found too similar to statements the Ninth Circuit's DRAM II decision had already held insufficient; executives' meetings at industry conferences, since DRAM II all but forecloses relying on them unless plaintiffs identify what was actually exchanged or agreed there; and the three-company market structure, which it called neutral. Answers are due Dec. 7, 2026, and the initial case management conference was reset for Jan. 12, 2027.

A federal judge on Nov. 14 refused to dismiss a proposed class action accusing Samsung, SK Hynix and Micron of conspiring to restrict the supply of conventional dynamic random-access memory, or DRAM, the standardized memory chips used in computers, phones and servers.

U.S. District Judge Noël Wise of the Northern District of California denied the companies' joint motion to dismiss in full, finding the complaint plausibly alleged an agreement in violation of Section 1 of the Sherman Act. The allegations, accepted as true at this stage, have not been proven.

The companies argued the case was a rerun of DRAM II, in which the Ninth Circuit in 2022 affirmed dismissal of claims against the same three companies over a 2016–2018 supply restriction. "The Court finds that it is not," Judge Wise wrote.

The suit was filed June 25, 2026, by 17 consumers and small businesses from five states. It concerns conventional DRAM, which the complaint describes as "standardized memory built to industry specifications and sold for ordinary purposes," including DDR5 generation modules built for computers.

According to the complaint, the three companies controlled more than 91% of global DRAM revenue as of the third quarter of 2025. They allegedly cut production starting in late 2022 and, beginning in 2023, shifted capacity to high bandwidth memory, or HBM, a specialized DRAM product for artificial intelligence accelerators that "requires approximately three to four times the silicon wafer area per gigabyte compared to conventional DDR5 DRAM."

By the third quarter of 2025, conventional DRAM prices had risen 171.8% in one year, according to the complaint, which alleges a 697% increase over 18 months. Yet "not one of the three Defendants expanded or announced plans to meaningfully expand commodity DRAM production capacity," the complaint alleges.

Without direct evidence of an agreement, the plaintiffs needed plus factors, additional facts suggesting a preceding agreement rather than conscious parallelism, in which competitors independently make similar moves.

Judge Wise rejected the companies' argument that timing gaps undercut parallel action. SK Hynix and Micron announced cuts three weeks apart in late 2022, she noted, and Samsung's lag of about four and a half months, until April 7, 2023, was "not such an unreasonably long delay that it defeats an allegation of parallel conduct on a motion to dismiss."

She found the complaint plausibly alleged that the three companies acted in parallel when they cut supply, shifted production from conventional DRAM such as DDR5 to HBM, and wound down DDR4.

Under Ninth Circuit precedent, action against self-interest must be "so perilous in the absence of advance agreement that no reasonable firm would make the challenged move without such an agreement." Judge Wise wrote that a pivot to HBM by itself "might not be sufficient," but that "the related conduct tips this factor over the edge to weigh in Plaintiffs' favor."

According to the complaint, all three signed long-term contracts locking in HBM supply, Samsung and SK Hynix reportedly refused long-term agreements with major conventional DRAM customers, and Micron announced on Dec. 3, 2025, that it would close Crucial, its 30-year-old consumer brand. Those moves, which she called "difficult if not impossible to unwind," plus the failure to expand despite record prices, "are the sort that at the pleading stage, it appears no reasonable firm would make without a prior agreement," she wrote.

She applied similar reasoning to allegations that Samsung and Micron delayed or halted new DRAM plants, citing the Ninth Circuit's 1990 Petroleum Products decision that "Changes in refinery capacity are not readily reversible." "The Court views the commitment to build or not build manufacturing capacity as analogous," she wrote. She also counted the companies' alleged same-quarter 2025 decisions to wind down DDR4 as a plus factor, citing the complaint's allegation that "older, slower DDR4 came to cost more per gigabyte than newer, faster DDR5."

Judge Wise found that near-identical customer-vetting practices all three companies allegedly adopted in January 2026 "strongly support a plausible inference of conspiracy." She rejected the companies' "obvious and non-conspiratorial explanation" of booming AI demand, noting that the vetting began after the AI boom and the HBM pivot were underway.

The court gave no weight to three other arguments. Judge Wise held that investor statements, including Micron's 2022 reference to "supply discipline," did not distinguish the case from DRAM II. Though the conference-meeting allegations went beyond those in DRAM II, she wrote that DRAM II "seemingly all but forecloses a trial court from giving any weight to trade conference meetings" absent specifics, and she called the market's oligopolistic structure "neutral in the analysis."

According to the complaint, the companies and two other manufacturers formed a criminal cartel to fix DRAM prices from 1998 to 2002; Samsung paid a $300 million fine, Hynix paid $185 million, and Micron received immunity for cooperating as a whistleblower. Judge Wise, like the DRAM II court, rejected the argument that the now-20-year-old history should not count.

At the hearing, the companies quoted the late Judge Posner's line that competitors in concentrated markets "watch each other like hawks." Judge Wise wrote: "But Plaintiffs' allegations go beyond hawks watching each other; their contentions are more akin to hawks flying in formation – an activity that hawks ordinarily do not do."

The plaintiffs are represented by Bathaee Dunne LLP. Samsung is represented by O'Melveny & Myers LLP, SK Hynix by Cleary Gottlieb Steen & Hamilton LLP, and Micron by Gibson, Dunn & Crutcher LLP.

Judge Wise ordered the companies to answer by Dec. 7, 2026. Because the court had reset argument by about three weeks, she also granted the companies' unopposed administrative motion to continue early case deadlines and reset the initial case management conference for Jan. 12, 2027, at 9 a.m.

item.title: My favourite modern NES games
item.description:
We are in the middle of the Second ReNESance (the first one is the one that saved the video game industry in North America). The combined decades of research and knowledge on how the venerable little NES works have produced a true cornucopia of games. We are all lucky to be here to witness it.

I am always happy to inform video game fans that the Nintendo Entertainment System is still receiving lots and lots of new third-party games.

In alphabetical order, because I refuse to rank them, here are 25 of my favourite modern NES games. Almost all can be obtained digitally, usually from the developer or publisher, most for a modest fee. Digital NES downloads are cheap! Most of these can also be obtained as physical cartridges for the true hi-fi experience on original hardware.

All Hell Unleashed

A little spooky, very pixelly. This game is a real gem.

Made by 8-bit Slasher who has been honing his skills in other horror games for the NES, All Hell Unleashed is an extensive love letter to the horror slashers of the 1980s and 1990s. There is an underlying story about an evil cult that is trying to resurrect something or other, but that’s just an excuse plot so that you can fight Jaws, Freddy, Jason, Ghostface and others. It works surprisingly well. You can select your favourite horror movie from a stage-select screen to do your platforming as you fight the forces of evil, culminating in the boss fights where the villain of each horror franchise swoops in for a mano-a-mano. The platforming feels good, and the boss fights function as set pieces showcasing the real villains we are here to see in their 8-bit glory.

Finally Jason dons a better outfit on the NES than that silly purple jumpsuit!

After each classic horror villain is defeated, it is time to take on the cult itself for one final showdown. Definitely a spine-tingling adventure!

Alwa’s Awakening

Alwa’s Awakening was originally a PC game made with pseudo-NES limitations (and in the case of the music, with actual NES limitations, as the developer used Famitracker to compose all of the music). If it doesn’t feel like a classic NES game and instead plays more like a modern indie Metroidvania, that’s because it is.

In the game, you play as Zoe, a girl who likes video games and one day awakens in the mystical land of Alwa, a place from one of her games. Your task is to guide Zoe through an adventure in Alwa where she will uncover power-ups that open up new avenues of adventure. Typical Metroidvania stuff, although a bit shorter than most games in the genre. The PC-to-NES port of this game was handled by my good friend Brad Smith of Lizard fame. He made a couple of interesting YouTube videos describing the process.

The game looks absolutely gorgeous for the NES, and its Famitracker-composed soundtrack made it through the porting process completely unscathed. There was a limited physical edition that today is only available via secondhand markets. If you can grab a copy, it’s a very high-quality production. This is some of the best stuff made for the system.

Cool boss fights too!

Anguna: Scourge of the Goblin King

Anguna is an NES game with an interesting lineage. It was originally made in 2008 for the Game Boy Advance as essentially the same game, but a bit more to the standards of the GBA. Then it was successively ported to the Nintendo DS, the Atari 2600, and finally the NES.

The Atari 2600-to-NES port was done fairly faithfully, which means that the design decisions necessary for the Atari also made it into the NES port. This means, for example, no more than two enemies per screen and always of the same type. This sort of restriction isn’t unheard of in the NES, though. The very popular NES Double Dragon port also has the same limitation. The game design makes up for it and overall results in an enjoyable experience. And isn’t that what making and playing modern NES games is all about? An interesting experience made with strict hardware limitations.

So what is Anguna? At its most basic, it’s a Zelda-like. You walk around screens, you grab new tools, your tools open new paths for exploration, you use the tools to fight monsters, with the most common tool in question being your trusty sword. You are a nameless warrior who is notably NOT called “Anguna” on a quest to defeat the goblin king. Usual bare-bones plot.

Most might consider this game to be short, but I would say it’s sleek and streamlined. It doesn’t do much, but what it does it does well.

Oh, one very important upgrade that the game got during the 2600-to-NES conversion: rockin’ enemy portraits in gorgeous 8-bit pixel art!

Blazing Rangers itch.io physical (N.B. The physical cartridge is shipped by 1st Press Games, who has had a spotty track record of fulfilling requests)

Blazing Rangers is single-screen arcade firefighting co-op action! The firefighting genre is under-explored in video games and Blazing Rangers manages to represent it admirably.

The goal is to rescue the children in each burning level and proceed to the next one. To do this you have to snake a powerful firehose that can blast both flames and baddies as you make your way to the children. You may also and often must drop your firehose and rely on your backpack with water in order to get to the further reaches of each level. There are powerups to collect, which give bonuses such as increasing the length of the hose or activating a sprinkler system that will slow the spread of fire throughout the level.

You can control either of two characters, Popo and Mimi, each with slight differences in gameplay. Popo is a bit slower but can recharge his backpack with water faster while Mimi is the other way around. Each level is timed, but you’re more likely to be overrun by flames or enemies than running out of time. The children can get singed by the fire but otherwise seem unharmed, unless you get burned carrying them, in which case they get burned too.

The game has a very catchy theme song that is also the BGM of each level.

Although it can be fun enough in single player, co-op is where the game really excels. It is very fun to coordinate with your partner as there is still only one hose in co-op. A strategy, for example, could be to have one player get the hose extension powerup that the other player can instantly use to take the hose a bit further into the flames.

Changeable Guardian Estique

Estique is a horizontal shmup with the distinct honour of being made by some of the original Compile developers, veterans of the shmup genre. This is noticeable in that it even uses some sound effects from Compile classics such as The Guardian Legend. In the game you pilot the eponymous super-robot that can transform between the bipedal mecha form that can recover damage more quickly or a sleek spaceship form that is more manoeuvrable and has a faster firing rate. Gameplay consists of carefully balancing between the two forms in the heat of battle depending on whether a more offensive or defensive approach is needed at the time.

The NES manual has a deliberately awkward English translation as a homage to the quality of writing we often encountered during the licensed era. Accordingly, the Japanese and English versions of the game are not identical, with the English version having mild censorship of the cut scenes, mimicking the restrictions that Nintendo used to impose on licensed NES games.

The game’s default difficulty is a little on the easy side, and the whole game can be completed in under an hour at the default difficulty. I get the impression that the intended difficulty is a bit higher, so you can always adjust it up for your gaming needs.

Regardless of the difficulty, the giant screen-filling boss fights are always a delight.

The Cowlitz Gamers’ 2nd Adventure

Why 2nd adventure, you might ask? Well, this game has an interesting history. The original adventure was written way back in 2015 to support the Arc of Cowlitz County charity. Within a couple of years, a sequel appeared and physical copies were made and distributed at the Portland Retro Gaming Expo. They aren’t made anymore, but if you’re exceedingly lucky, you might be able to nab a second-hand copy somewhere. Finally the game was uploaded to itch.io as a free download, with a nudge to donate to the charity.

The game is a tightly-made single-screen arcade platformer where siblings Kaylee and Justice decide to go down into the mines and see who can collect the most gold and diamonds to buy fireworks for the festivities. It can be played co-op or single-player, where the co-op is also half competitive mode to see who can pick up the most gems. The siblings have no way to directly attack any of the enemies in the mines, so it’s all up to careful jumping and dodging to clear each screen of gold in order to open the way up to the next screen.

The platforming is responsive and engaging. Very fun to play. It’s no surprise then that this game has achieved some popularity with speedrunners.

The music is a real standout and full of earworms. Several chiptune artists contributed to this game’s vibrant soundtrack. I often find myself humming the tune of the first few levels. Sometimes I even go into the options screen where the sound test lets me play all of the game’s tunes and use it as my jukebox.

The game’s colourful graphics perfectly complement the music.

Data Man

Okay, before we go on, I have to point out this game’s hilarious retro-themed trailer.

Those two kids furiously mashing the buttons always give me a laugh. That’s exactly the same look I have when I play this game.

Data Man is an arena shooter in the style of Xeno Crisis or Smash TV. Like most arena shooters, a second player can join in to fight all the baddies. Unlike most arena shooters, you don’t actually die if the baddies get to you, because what you are trying to defend isn’t yourself, but the very chips of your NES.

You see, bugs have invaded your NES. They are going for your CPU! You must defend your CPU at all costs before the bugs manage to eat their way through it. There are little bugs, big bugs, boss bugs, and they are all trying to chomp onto your CPU. You will only be momentarily stunned and lose some of your firepower if the bugs injure you. Their real target is your computer’s chips. You can blow up capacitors if need be, and their explosions can take out some bugs. That’s okay. Defend your CPU from waves and waves of bugs in order to clear the current level!

Should you fail in your mission and the bugs manage to wreck your CPU, your very NES will be unable to continue and you will be treated to a glitch fest of a game over.

I find the game rather difficult in single player and more enjoyable in co-op. If you can find a friend to play with you, I recommend doing so.

Dungeons and DoomKnights

This game has high production values. It’s an 8-bit spinoff of the AdventureQuest universe, a universe that recently obtained the distinction of being the most over-funded Kickstarter ever (their funding goal was one dollar, so each dollar added 100% more to their funding goal, haha).

It is a game that doesn’t and also does take itself seriously. There is serious gameplay here, as our hero Artix and his deadly pomeranian explore a world plagued by the undead and the infernal. There are both top-down and side view action sequences, lots of action, and lots of secrets to explore. The exploration is fun, the action is fun, and I am very glad this game exists. They crafted a world with many nooks and crannies to discover.

Should you get the physical version, you’re in for a treat. Artix Entertainment took lots of care to ensure you got a complete package. You’ll get the game, feelies, a certificate, and a copy of Pretendo Empower, (also available digitally) where you can read about all the lore and secrets of this game.

Battle on!

Garbage Pail Kids: Mad Mike and the Quest for Stale Gum

Remember the Garbage Pail Kids? The gross-out cards that were a parody of Cabbage Patch kids, created by Art Spiegelman, the same Art Spiegelman who made the poignant and award-winning Maus? Well, what if the Garbage Pail Kids branched out into one of the most popular media of their heyday, the NES?

I’ll admit, when I first watched the trailer mockumentary, I was briefly deceived that this was an actual game that was recently unearthed.

This is an NES game alright, although an actual NES copy is rather elusive. There was a run of physical NES cartridges made by iam8bit but it was sold out long ago. There is no digital distribution of the actual NES ROM although the Steam version does seem to have the actual ROM hidden in there somewhere, with Cowabunga reportedly being able to extract it. The second-hand market seems to be the only way to get a physical copy nowadays.

As to playing the game, gross-out humour and every sort of bodily excretion is of course the main attraction. It’s a very well-made exploration platformer where you can switch between four of the titular kids, each with their own disgusting abilities.

Mad Mike can fight with his axe and sword. Leaky Lindsay can fling boogers at the enemies. Luke Puke’s vomit projectiles downwards instead, sort of like Simon Belmont’s holy water, but a lot less holy. And Patty Putty is an extra-bouncy baby who jumps high and stomps down butt-first with a full diaper.

Retrotainment programmed the game, with many years of NES experience, and it shows. The game plays and controls beautifully and the level design is interesting, with close fidelity to the source material.

Gunhawk

People are still experimenting with NES peripherals. People such as Hexcellent have worked on Power Pad-based glitch art installations* . Micro Mages has given new life to 4-player adapters, and if they ever finish it, even RAD vs Dragons will breathe new life into ROB the NES Robot.

For the venerable Zapper, we have Gunhawk. The game is controlled either with gamepad to dodge and the Zapper to aim and shoot, or it can be controlled with just the gamepad alone, using the B button to shoot and holding down the A button to dodge. The intended experience does seem to be with the Zapper, as I found it more difficult to use the gamepad because you cannot aim and dodge at the same time.

We take the pilot’s seat of an experimental mecha stolen and commandeered by Nue, who has stolen the titular Gunhawk in order to escape from some vaguely evil military base. Emma, a local resistance leader, will contact us in levels with cut scenes that advance the story. You have to clear waves of enemies with various movements and attack patterns. Your shot charges automatically in a way that reminds me of the Battle Clash games for the SNES that used the Super Scope. Boss enemies also make an appearance at the end of each sector, and there are upgrades to obtain as well as taking a gamble in hacking scenes between levels (no hacking minigame, as far as I can tell, it’s just a dice roll if your hacking will succeed or fail).

Here is Y.T. showing how the game is played.

The gameplay is challenging and varied. The gamepad + zapper control scheme is effective. If you decide to get the physical version, you will get secrets in the manual that can be read with a red filter as was the style at the time.

* Which despite being, well, “(h)excellent”, I did not include in this list because it’s more of glitch art toy than a game.

GunTneR

From the madcap dreams of Langel Bookbinder (this guy) comes GunTneR, a crazy fun horizontal shmup that goes RIGHT-TO-LEFT (seriously, what kind of shmup goes in that direction? I can’t think of any other!)

In GunTneR we pilot the Rudy, a ship of the titular GunTneR class across the “13th dimension”… actually, y’know what, let’s just leave the explanation to the manual:

I crack up every time I read that, yes, including right now as I’m writing this. Bookbinder’s peculiar sense of humour shines through in this game.

And the game is fun to play too. It’s a timed mission to take a Dingle to some sort of space veterinarian or something. The sooner you get there, the healthier your Dingle will be. You have to clear out each wave of baddies, carefully balancing your ship’s shield levels with the occasional frenetic rapid-fire burst you can activate to help you clear out the current wave. There is a power-up juggle mechanic similar to Konami’s Pop’n Twinbee bells that can help you keep a power-up on the screen to be collected at a later time as may be convenient. You will receive “congrations” after clearing each boss enemy.

There is so much going on at once that it’s sometimes hard to keep up, but with some practice you can learn what needs to be dodged, what needs to be shot, and what needs to be collected.

And look! I’m a low-dimensional fan!

Haunted: Halloween Trilogy

Three times now since 2015, the Retrotainment team has regaled us with a Halloween adventure right on time, an irregular tradition for October 31st.

In the first game we take control of Donny Johnstown, elementary-school aged-kid who has to battle the undead forces of Haunted Harry over many levels of undead platforming horror in the town of Possum Hollow. In ’86, now in middle school, Tami can join the fray via co-op tag-team action. This actually introduces a sort of hidden co-op mode, as a second player holding the second gamepad can hit select at any time to tag in. This mechanic returns in ’87, along with some non-linearity to the level selection as well as some added shmup sections on a flying broom. It is the year of the Witch, after all.

The three games have an overarching story as Donny and Tami discover more of the mystery of Possum Hollow and thrice thwart the thanatological throngs and theatrics of Haunted Harry. The ’86 game grows Donny’s and Tami’s move set letting you choose an upgrade at the end of each level, and the full arsenal is available from the beginning in ’87. The polish across the three games gradually increases as Retrotainment hones their craft. They are well-designed platformers, with beautiful background art and spritework and tight, responsive controls. The three games in unison craft a perfect spooky atmosphere for any Halloween.

I gotta say, of all the methods that fiction has come up with for dealing with the undead, drop-kicking them or decapitating them with a well-placed uppercut is one of the more novel ones.

Jane Austen’s 8-bit Adventure itch.io Steam Nintendo store (Physical versions sold out, but the authors have made vague promises of another possible future run of cartridges)

It sounds like a joke,

but it’s a surprisingly well-made game.

Being a fan of Jane Austen’s work isn’t a prerequisite, but it helps to be acquainted in order to grasp some of the details and setting of this game. The gameplay is quintessential NES platforming, with good controls and an interesting central mechanic. It’s not too difficult or too long, but it’s not short either. It feels just right with just the right amount of challenge.

The story is that Jane Austen finds herself in an unfamiliar 8-bit world and characters she portrayed unfavourably in her books are her main antagonists. Using her quill to attack (which after all, is mightier than the sword) and collecting cups of tea for ammunition, she must traverse platforming levels inspired by each of her novels until she can find a way out of this world.

It all sounds rather silly but it works very well and the game is actually quite fun. Although my knowledge of Jane Austen begins and ends with Clueless and “it is a truth universally acknowledged…“, the game gave me a desire to read more of her work.

Lizard My lizard is the lizard of tagline

Put on a lizard and go on an adventure!

My lizard is the lizard of reminiscence

Lizard for me is a very personal and emotional game. I met the author Brad Smith via this game and we have since become good friends. We play video games almost every week and chat about whatever is crossing our minds. And that feels a lot like what Lizard feels like. Lizard is a meandering, personal, somewhat aimless game. Sometimes I joke that it’s just Brad’s mad science experiment on human brains. Lizard presents you with challenges, puzzles, discovery, and frustration and makes no attempt to dictate how you should react: surprise, determination, desperation. Lizard just sits there quietly waiting to see your ensuing feelings.

My lizard is the lizard of lore

I should explain at this point what the gameplay actually is. It’s an open-world exploration platformer. Lizard dumps you in the middle of a world that gives you no objective and no explanation save what you can find on your own. You begin by wearing the Lizard of Knowledge and if you read the manual you can get some pointers that there are other lizards you may discover. There is no direction you should specifically explore, and the denizens of Lizard seem downright disinterested in you.
