With narrow exceptions you cannot hurt them, and they will not attack you unless you approach them. Everyone was simply minding their business until you showed up wearing a lizard.

The game actually feels oneiric because it sort of is inspired by a dream. One of Brad’s friends once awoke from a dream, distressed and proclaiming, “my lizard is not the lizard of knowledge! My lizard is not the lizard of knowledge!!“. Curious to discover what the Lizard of Knowledge might be and what other lizards there may be, Brad spent years making this game.

My lizard is the lizard of multimedia

Lizard is an NES game, but it has also been ported to many other platforms. For me, however, the full Lizard experience includes all the supplemental materials Brad has provided, most of which can be found on his website. Therein you can find source code for the game, developer blog posts, videos explaining how the game was made, cheats, and so much more. Lizard is an NES game, but it’s an NES game that is keenly self-aware that it is a modern NES game, and that people are allowed to experience it however they see fit. You can play a superficial platformer or you can engage deeply with its secrets.

MicroMages

Ah, Micro Mages… probably one of the most explosively popular modern NES games. Hey, there’s a good chance that you’ve already seen its making-of video, and if you haven’t, now is always a good time to do so:

In the world of modern NES games, Micro Mages has become an institution. The premise is simple: four mages teleport to the fortress atop Pretzel Mountain to save their beloved Princess. You can shoot, charge shoot, jump, and wall-jump. That’s your lot. Now go and fight the forces of evil!

What makes people love Micro Mages is how well it all works together in such a, well, micro package. The Morphcat duo of Nicolas Bétoux and Julius Riecke created a real masterpiece. The gameplay is engaging, just the right difficulty curve, with perfectly-designed levels that gradually ramp up challenge. The game also has the rare distinction of being a 4-player game, and it’s an absolute blast to play it that way. The four mages can push each other, which can both help and hinder gameplay depending on how you play. Will you help your fellow mage reach the top of the tower, or will you selfishly push them into the abyss and collect the treasures by yourself?

The neat thing is that dying in co-op doesn’t mean you’re out of the game. Downed mages become ghosts, and if you find the right power-up you can come back to life. In the meantime, they can help the live mages by temporarily freezing baddies with their spectral shots. All mages share a single life counter, which only goes down if there are no surviving mages left in that attempt.

It has become a sort of tradition at my household that new guests get to experience at least some Micro Mages co-op with my family on original hardware.

The game has been around for a while, so it may have already been ported to your modern console of choice, including Switch, PS4, and PS5.

Lastly, if you can’t get enough Micro Mages and you want more levels, you can either try the Second Quest (a sort of DLC released by Morphcat) or Micro Mages Maker!

OverObj physical (sold out, no other way to buy this game)

(All right, this game is no longer available from its original seller. But it’s too good for me not to mention it. Maybe there will be another way to purchase it some day.)

In Europe and America, the predominant genre for modern NES games is platformers. In the Japanese scene, shmups abound (or “STG” as they call them over there, “Shoo Ting Game”). Amidst Japanese shmups, a particularly popular genre is the bullet hell. Complex bullet patterns on screen and the primary gameplay is carefully weaving your spaceship or character through the bullets while you continuously fire back.

On the Famicom, bullet hell games are difficult to develop because the NES has room for only 64 sprite entries in its graphics memory, and can display only eight sprites per horizontal row. Nintendo developers used to refer to these sprites as “OBJ”.

Game developer Little Sound thus found a little trick to get over the OBJ limit: split the sprites across the middle of the screen and update the sprite data partway through rendering a frame.

It sounds like a tech demo, but this game is actually loads of fun. The difficulty quickly ramps up, but every time my little spaceship blows up, it feels like it was a genuine mistake and the game is being fair. The later bosses and levels do suffer from some sprite flickering despite OverObj’s technical feats. I love weaving through the bullet patterns, and that’s what keeps me coming back.

There’s also some excuse plot about how the Earth, after being abandoned by humans, is being attacked by mindless Objects that started breeding on their own, while being defended by lonely android who is waiting for makers who will never return.

Yeah, heavy stuff. Anyway, weave through the bullet storm, shoot back, and marvel at the joy of a well-made bullet hell on the NES.

Project Blue

Project Blue is mechanically simply a platformer. Run, jump, shoot, get to the end of the level. There is no scrolling, but there is a sprawling map to explore, which is mostly linear. There is not much in the way of branching paths. The mechanics are good enough with a peculiarity about jumping where you need to get a running start to gain more jumping height. It works well enough.

Where the game really stands out is in its presentation. The box art and manual were made by the likes of M-Tee, a veteran of modern NES art. The level design and graphics were made by FrankenGraphics, a designer with a unique sense of dark, detailed artistry who has been working on the NEXXT tool for NES graphics. Her style is instantly recognisable as she is able to cram surprising amounts of detail that seem impossible for the limitations of the NES. Rounding up the team is toggleswitch who handled the code and design.

Together they created a cyberpunk story about Blue who is a test subject escaping the OmniCorp labs by jumping and shooting and dealing with the literal Think Tanks of OmniCorp’s board of directors.

The visuals are interesting and do give the sense of an oppressive biotech lab run by robots and cyborgs, as well as some outdoor shots of Neo Hong Kong where the story unfolds.

The music does a great job setting the foreboding atmosphere. I also get quite the kick out of its PDF manual, which is presented as being a scan of the actual manual. It looks like it was scanned in some dingy basement, because a cockroach managed to sneak onto the scanner bed!

The gameplay is somewhat comparable to Battle Kid but much more forgiving. Less trial-and-death gameplay, more fun running around dodging and shooting.

Sam’s Journey

Sam’s Journey tells the tale of little Sam who one day gets snatched from his bedroom and lands in a strange and wondrous land that he must make his way out of! Along the way he can find several outfits that all have their own special abilities.

For example, Disco Sam can spin which slows down his fall, and Vampire Sam can temporarily transform into a bat and fly around the level.

The game play is multidirectional platforming in a style that I cannot help but compare with Super Mario Bros. 3, and yes, I think the game is at least as good as the best games on the NES. It is a curious thing, because Sam’s Journey was originally made for the Commodore 64, with the NES port coming later. I have not played the original C64 version (to be honest, the pastel colours of the C64 are less appealing to me), but I think some of the “flavour” of the C64 shows through. There’s a certain style of platformer I associate with platforms such as the Amiga or the C64 which were more popular in Europe than America, which makes me call Sam’s Journey a sort of Europlatformer. This is by no means a criticism, as the game’s levels require exploration, but are nevertheless mostly linear. The goal in each level is simply to find the flashing door representing the exit, using whatever power-ups are scattered in each level.

Between levels there is a level-select world map reminiscent of SMB3 or MC Kids, although it’s rather perfunctory. There is no branching possible and all of the levels have to be completed in strict order. The only purpose of this world map is to backtrack to a previous level to search for more hidden collectibles.

You see, each level has exactly 40 gems, 10 coins, and 3 trophies. Finding all of those collectibles in each level is how you obtain the 100% completion rate for the level. If you just want to get to the exit, the path is usually clear, but if you want to explore and find how the level designers hid all of the collectibles in each level, that’s also another way to play. I opted for the completionist route, just because I was having so much fun exploring every last cranny and nook of each level.

Thankfully the game has a save feature, which is quite welcome for the completionist. Even the speedrunner will have quite a game on their hands with WhiteHat94’s speedrun clocking at 47:23:

Each level is essentially a little self-contained adventure. Sam keeps his current outfit from one level to the next, but after playing through the whole game I could never find a place where an outfit was required to progress but not available in the current level. Of course outfits such as Vampire Sam were useful for more easily exploring all levels with its flying ability, but it was by no means required. I particularly enjoyed how each outfit had its use and the level design does a great job showcasing the need for all of Sam’s abilities.

Lastly, should you get the physical edition of this game, expect high quality. The box comes with a comprehensive manual, feelies, and there is even a hidden collectible somewhere in the physical package! Knight of Bytes poured lots of love into this game which is why I love it too.

Slow Mole

Let’s begin with the cutesy claymation commercial:

Poor little claymation mole. I personally do not feel that sort of frustration with trial-and-death gameplay. For me, it’s an experience of focus and meditation.

Slow Mole is a precision platformer with a unique twist: your mole is slow, the world is fast. If you want to have a checkpoint past the current screen, you need to complete the current screen under a time limit.

Together, these mechanics create an environment where you have infinite tries to perfectly nail a little speedrunning challenge screen by screen, repeatedly dying until you get just the right rhythm. Once you do so, it’s greatly satisfying to have guided the little critter onto the next screen.

There is lots of variety in the obstacles and environments. The novelty of discovery keeps rewarding the player with each screen that was cleared. Every section is a new challenge and the game spices it up. A must play for fans of precision platformers!

The Storied Sword

Mix Ninja Gaiden-style cut scenes, NES-Batman-like wall-jumping, and Princess Bride-like story, all set to the expert tunes of Raftronaut, and you get The Storied Sword!

The evil sorcerer Vectre seeks the Storied Sword in order to break his curse and remember the name of his one true love. In order to stop the evil despot, Cedric the Candlemaster and Orchid of Mourning team up to traverse the Storm Coast and prevent Vectre’s brigands from stealing the Sword for their master. The story progresses in twists and turns through cinematic cut scenes between levels as we learn more of what became of Vectre, his generals, and our two heroes.

The game is a fast-paced platformer with a unique character thanks to its wall-jumping mechanics. You have infinite attempts to get through each checkpoint. After each death you can pick a different hero, as they do differ slightly in gameplay. Cedric slices forward with his sword and throws daggers, while Orchid cuts more vertically and has a short-range boomerang-like weapon.

The infinite attempts give it a slight trial-and-death feel. As I played the game, I ended up routing mini-speedruns through each section. I discovered that it’s possible to consistently play the levels until you memorise an optimal path. For the latter levels of the game, this became essential as stopping to take a breath could mean death, because the rapid rate of enemies spawning would quickly overwhelm me. Completing the game felt very satisfying and I enjoyed the feel of the platforming mechanics as well as the flourish of the story.

There are surprises for those who complete the game, so I do recommend persisting until you come face-to-face with Vectre. It’s an adventure well worth experiencing!

Super Bat Puncher Demo

Morphcat’s entire catalogue is fantastic and Super Bat Puncher Demo is no exception. It is called “demo” because originally Morphcat intended to expand it to a larger game, but has since given up that promise. Regardless, the game that exists is novel and interesting. It teases more game content that never came.

It is also a very silly game. You take control of Captain Roast of the BEEF (Bat-Excommunication and Eradication Force) who can team up with a second player controlling Sir Loin (a flying yellow bird) to take out the explosive bats of planet BAT before they destroy Earth.

Yeah, the story is ridiculous, but the gameplay is tight!

In this little platforming adventure, Captain Roast’s primary weapon is an extending punching glove that he can use to attack the bats of planet BAT. Along the way there are upgrades to uncover such as the bowling ball rolling attack or the wall boost. Each one grants new ways to navigate through the planet and deal with the many baddies within, which aren’t limited to just bats.

Besides the main route, there is a hidden expert area where you can really push Captain Roast’s abilities to the limit and show who is the best bat puncher of them all.

Wonderful as it is, the game is nevertheless very short and has left the entire fanbase hungry for more. Alas, it seems unlikely that it will ever be expanded to the full game that was once promised.

Super Tilt Bro

Super Smash Bros for your NES with online multiplayer. That’s the pitch. But how can the NES, a console that predates online gaming services, do this?

One of the wonderful features of the NES that gave it much of its longevity during the Nintendo-licensed era and into the present age is that it is always possible to augment its capabilities via extra hardware in NES cartridges. This happened pretty quickly in the 1980s as cartridges used fancy memory mappers to increase the amount of data that an NES game could use. In modern times, people realised that there’s no theoretical limit to how much the extra hardware in an NES cartridge could do, so why not stick a wifi chip in there?

With this, it’s time to flesh out the game.

Super Tilt Bro’s base game is about four characters from the open source and video game worlds battling for supremacy. There is Sinbad, the mascot of the OGRE 3d rendering engine, Pepper and Carrot of David Revoy’s art, Kiki the Krita mascot, and the Video Game Sage of the eponymous message board. If you install the latest DLC as of this writing, you will also get Sunny of Super Sunny World. (I’m very amused that she first appeared in a side game before her own game was officially launched.)

It is a thrilling novelty to see your humble NES connect to the internet and download an update to get a new character or the latest improvements.

The game has gone through many rounds of rebalancing so that each character feels good to play. It also supports cross-play with its free web version hosted on itch.io (with rollback netplay, natch), so as long as you can find an opponent, there is always a way to play. There is also a single-player story campaign, but of course the online features are the big draw.

Regular tournaments are still being held as of this writing. Maybe I’ll see you there some day!

The Trial of Kharzoid

It sounds a bit crazy that you can just jam together any two genres and get a good game, but that’s exactly what happened here: Pascal Belisle combined Arkanoid with exploration that expands as you acquire abilities, creating an Arkanoidvania.

Here is an interview. In the second half, the Kharzoid author describes his game.

The story is that the maleficent necromancer Kharzoid has devised a diabolical trial in which hapless victims are reduced to their skulls and forced to endure a dungeon full of monsters. Nobody has won the trial, but our nameless hero decides to submit himself to the Trial in hopes of breaking Kharzoid’s grip over the people and killing him once and for all.

The Trial, of course, is your skull bouncing around with the help of a paddle or paddles as is traditional in Breakout/Arkanoid mechanics. The game keeps the core mechanic fresh while adding an exploration element. After each board is cleared, you can pick which direction to explore in the dungeon and see what other ordeal lies within. The atmosphere is suitably spooky, and the exploration is more than a gimmick: you encounter townsfolk and find upgrades along the way, both of which provide invaluable aid against the horrors that Kharzoid has in store for you.

The boss fights do not disappoint either. If you’ve ever heard of Strikey Sisters or Firestriker and you enjoyed them, give Kharzoid a try too… or a trial.

Twin Dragons

Funny thing, this game was the first one that clued me in to the existence of modern NES games. The game came out in 2017. It tells the story of Dinky and Minky, the titular dragons, on their quest to rescue their unhatched sibling from the sorcerer who stole the egg.

Mechanically, it is a conventional horizontally scrolling platformer. You begin controlling Dinky, the green dragon, and complete a few levels. Then you play a few levels as his sister Minky. After collecting the appropriate power-up, Dinky can breathe high-powered fireballs, while Minky can shoot ice blasts and fly. After a few levels, the two dragons reunite and you can freely change between them at any time in order to clear the final levels.

For me, this game’s claim to fame is that it kickstarted the creation of Homebrew Factory, an enterprise that has been running for a few years now, cranking out physical copies of many other games for the NES and other retro consoles. I first obtained this game and realised that people were creating full-fledged adventures on the old console, worthy of consideration.

The game itself is fun. I enjoy its mechanics, its slightly unusual story (rescuing eggs instead of princesses is a new one), and the overall challenge it presents. The visuals and soundtrack are appealing. I am grateful that Twin Dragons paved the way for other NES games.

Undercover Shot

This game has a very simple but original premise. It requires two players. One controls the undercover impostor with a gamepad and selects their outfit’s colour. The second player has to shoot the impostor with a Zapper. Yes, it’s a Zapper game!

There are four characters on screen, and they all move in semi-random patterns. The impostor has to move like an NPC and go unnoticed. If the shooter hits the impostor, the shooter wins. Otherwise, if the shooter hits an innocent bystander, the impostor wins.

That’s all. Each round is a brief game of cat-and-mouse. There is no score, no ultimate goal, no story. One player has to move like an NPC; the other has to shoot the character who moves most suspiciously. Simple!

It’s a great party game. Grab a bunch of people and take turns playing the shooter and the impostor. This game was a big hit when I gave it to a bunch of kids during a birthday party. They were having lots of fun figuring out how the Zapper works, how the NPCs move, how to outsmart each other. If you ever want to liven up a gathering, try playing this game for a little while!

item.title: Disk encryption on NetBSD – achieving secrecy
item.description:
Threat models

These are two threat models for which disk encryption is the answer:

The device is stolen or lost and its contents must remain secret.

The device is tampered with, and all attempts at tampering must render it unusable.

Right now, we will focus on the first threat model. It is very difficult to build a tamper-proof system, and you need to worry about tamper-proofing your hardware, depending on what kind of actor is a realistic threat.

If we want to keep data on the system secret, we must first consider which data is worth protecting. On a NetBSD system, our data can be grouped into two broad categories:

System files (open source software)

User-modified files

Does the /bin/sh executable downloaded from the NetBSD FTP server contain any sensitive information?

On a BSD system, due to the separation of the base system and packages, many root file system directories are mostly unmodified outside of upgrades. In a properly configured system, nearly all system daemons and user applications are not going to be running as root, so won’t have permission to modify or create files in /bin.

We can reasonably assume that /bin/sh is the same binary that every other NetBSD user is running. A user may even opt to make directories containing such system files read-only.

Problems with disk encryption

The operating system needs to be able to load files to boot.[citation needed] This makes "true" full disk encryption difficult to achieve without specialized hardware, since the user needs some way to enter a password or an encryption key, and can’t do so without some form of software running on their computer. NetBSD also needs to store some amount of metadata about the encrypted partition on the disk, such as information on how to generate a secure 256-bit key from a 24 character password.

It is common for Unix systems to use shared libraries, which are loaded by programs to access system functionality. If these become unavailable, for example, by /usr/lib going missing, it becomes much harder to use the system. Familiarize yourself with the standard utilities in /rescue which don’t need working shared libraries to be useful.

The cryptographic algorithms that get standardized by the US government tend to be slow when implemented in software. This carries a performance penalty. As a result, many modern CPUs include implementations of ciphers like AES in hardware. For those that don’t, there’s alternative ciphers like Adiantum.

Which directories are sensitive?

And which are necessary for the OS to load?

On a normal NetBSD system, several directories have a high chance of being modified during system operation:

/home - user-specific files

/var - log files, system-wide databases (e.g. mail notifications), crash dumps…

/root - configuration files relevant to the root user account

/usr/pkg and /usr/local - where third-party software is installed

/etc - init scripts, system-wide configuration for the base system

A simple approach might be to encrypt /home. However, this might not be enough for some users. Although the crash directory can be easily changed with sysctl, a crash dump contains a snapshot of system memory which might be sensitive. If any servers have been run on the system, the log files might be sensitive. Mail sent to users (e.g. about their interrupted vi sessions and associated backups) might reveal sensitive file names.

Some users opt for the cgdroot approach, which uses only a small unencrypted ramdisk to pivot to an encrypted file system. However, this modifies the system startup routines significantly and may make certain rescue options harder. So, it’s worth asking whether there’s an approach that is somewhere in the middle, and still uses the standard NetBSD installation and boot process. Many BSD systems use separate file system partitions for /usr and /var, and this is a standard configuration supported by the NetBSD installer.

/etc is a harder problem to solve, since it contains files necessary to boot the system. However, on a typical desktop system, many files in /etc remain untouched. Passwords in /etc are generally stored only in hash form, except for Wi-Fi access points and certain VPN configurations (although it’s easy to reconfigure wpa_supplicant_flags to use a different configuration file from the default one in /etc). Many configuration files are only loaded much later in the boot process, after /usr is already mounted, and can easily be replaced with symbolic links to files on another file system.

The installation process

The NetBSD installer has basic functionality, but gets the job done quickly. In this configuration, we’re going to install NetBSD to a small unencrypted root file system. When you start to ignore the growth that can occur in /usr and /var and /home, even a complete NetBSD installation with development tools included is tiny. 4 GB should be more than enough.

For example purposes, I am going to use a sparc64 virtual machine, but the process is basically the same for more mainstream CPU architectures like amd64.

The installer detects that we already have a partitioned disk. We’re going to pick the "e: Delete everything" option so we have a fresh disk to start with:

Next, we’re going to choose "Set sizes of NetBSD partitions". This will allow us to have a small root, and reserve a large encrypted partition:

Here, I’ve decided I want a 4096 MB (4 GB) root file system, and a 11263 MB (11 GB) partition allocated for /var. Later, we’ll make /usr and /var share a disk partition, so don’t worry about this too much. Select "Go on".

On the next screen, I’ve changed the type of the secondary partition to "cgd" (listed under "Other type"), NetBSD’s encrypted device driver. I’ve also set its mount point to "-" so we can reconfigure it later:

I tell the installer I want to do a Full Installation and it completes as normal, installing everything into the small root partition.

When we reboot and log in as root, we enter a new world… our 4 GB unencrypted root partition.

Post-installation setup (disklabel)

Note

 Disklabel partitions are supported by every NetBSD port, and are required by some ports, such as sparc64 in our example. However, if your system uses UEFI, or you opted to use GPT partitions in the installer, your system has disk wedges instead. Ignore this section and read the section below for information about wedges.

Since I’m on sparc64, the disk is partitioned into disklabels. wd0 is the primary drive, and the disklabel command shows that /dev/wd0d is the partition reserved for our encrypted file system:

# disklabel wd0 # size offset fstype [fsize bsize cpg/sgs] a: 8389584 0 4.2BSD 0 0 0 # (Cyl. 0 - 8322) b: 2097152 8389584 swap # (Cyl. 8323 - 10403*) c: 33554432 0 unused 0 0 # (Cyl. 0 - 33288*) d: 23067072 10487232 cgd # (Cyl. 10404 - 33287)

We can go directly ahead with creating a parameters file for the cgd:

# cgdconfig -g -k argon2id -o /etc/cgd/wd0d adiantum 256

And then load the configuration and set our password:

# cgdconfig -V re-enter cgd0 /dev/wd0d

Now cgd0 appears to the system as yet another disk, but all attempts to access that disk will be automatically encrypted/decrypted by the kernel.

The next time we enter our password, we want to be able to verify that the password was correct, to avoid reading or writing invalid data.

This is done by choosing a verification method based on the contents of the encrypted partition. For flexibility’s sake, we’re going to put another disklabel inside the encrypted partition. This will allow the system to easily verify the password is correct by looking for a valid disklabel, but also gives us flexibility in our choice of file system.

# disklabel -i cgd0

This opens the interactive editor. We’re going to enter N to set a name for our disklabel (enter something like "cgdlabel"), then enter a to modify the first sub-partition.

First, it asks for a file system type. Enter ? to display a list of types:

partition>a Filesystem type [unused]: ? Supported file system types:

Since I’m running -current and want to test the Log File System, I’m going to enter "4.4LFS". A more common and well-tested configuration would be "4.2BSD".

Next is the start offset and partition size:

Start offset ('x' to start after partition 'x') [0c, 0s, 0M]: 0 Partition size ('$' for all remaining) [0c, 0s, 0M]: $

Since "a" is the only sub-partition at the moment, the default start of 0 is fine. "$" will use all available space on the cgd.

Finally, we’ll save our new label and quit the disklabel editor:

partition>W Label disk [n]?y Label written partition>Q

Now change the verify_method in /etc/cgd/wd0d to disklabel, and add a line in /etc/cgd/cgd.conf to create the cgd at boot time:

cgd0 /dev/wd0d /etc/cgd/wd0d

We can now access this hidden partition as /dev/cgd0a. But for it to be useful, we’ll need to create a file system on it. Once again, here I’m using the Log File System:

# newfs_lfs /dev/rcgd0a

A more normal and well-tested configuration would be FFSv2ea:

# newfs -O2ea /dev/rcgd0a

We can now mount and access the encrypted file system:

# mkdir -p /encfs # mount /dev/cgd0a /encfs

Add a new line in /etc/fstab for our encrypted mount point:

/dev/cgd0a /encfs lfs rw,noatime 1 2

Use "ffs" instead of "lfs" if you aren’t using the Log File System. If using FFS, you may want to use the options rw,log,noatime to enable journaling.

Post-installation setup (disk wedges)

On a recent amd64 machine, your system probably uses GPT and disk wedges instead of disklabels. Assuming our primary disk is ld0, we can see a list of wedges with dkctl:

# dkctl ld0 listwedges /dev/rld0: 3 wedges: dk0: 20e57277-ad70-408e-9c68-225270ed1500, 9267072 blocks at 64, type: ffs dk1: abad5a2d-8411-4d36-980e-a5f2b03a1047, 4194304 blocks at 9267136, type: swap dk2: 2c4d136a-f7ed-48f8-aae8-38afdd50c661, 53647360 blocks at 13461440, type: cgd

Note

 If your disk is SATA rather than NVMe, it’s probably called wd0 instead of ld0.

In this case, our partition reserved for our encrypted file system is /dev/dk2, also accessible via the UUID alias NAME=2c4d136a-f7ed-48f8-aae8-38afdd50c661.

We can go directly ahead with creating a parameters file for the cgd:

# cgdconfig -g -k argon2id -o /etc/cgd/maincgd aes-cbc 256

And then load the configuration and set our password:

# cgdconfig -V re-enter cgd0 NAME=2c4d136a-f7ed-48f8-aae8-38afdd50c661 /etc/cgd/maincgd

Now cgd0 appears to the system as yet another disk, but all attempts to access that disk will be automatically encrypted/decrypted by the kernel.

The next time we enter our password, we want to be able to verify that the password was correct, to avoid reading or writing invalid data.

This is done by choosing a verification method based on the contents of the encrypted partition. For flexibility’s sake, we’re going to put another GPT partition table inside the encrypted partition. This will allow the system to easily verify the password is correct by looking for a valid GPT table, but also gives us flexibility in our choice of file system.

# gpt create cgd0

Now change the verify_method in /etc/cgd/maincgd to gpt, and add a line in /etc/cgd/cgd.conf to create the cgd at boot time:

cgd0 NAME=2c4d136a-f7ed-48f8-aae8-38afdd50c661 /etc/cgd/maincgd

For now, we’ll only create one partition inside the new sub-table. I’m running -current and want to test the Log File System, so I’ll use the "lfs" partition type. A more common and well-tested configuration would be "ffs".

# gpt add -l encfs -t lfs cgd0

You should receive a kernel message, readable with the dmesg command, which notes that a new wedge is available, including its number. In this case, it’s dk3.

For it to be useful, we’ll need to create a file system on it. Once again, here I’m using the Log File System:

# newfs_lfs /dev/rdk3

A more normal and well-tested configuration would use FFSv2ea:

# newfs -O2ea NAME=encfs

We can now mount and access the encrypted file system:

# mkdir -p /encfs # mount NAME=encfs /encfs

Add a new line in /etc/fstab for our encrypted mount point:

NAME=encfs /encfs lfs rw,noatime 1 2

Use "ffs" instead of "lfs" if you aren’t using the Log File System. If using FFS, you may want to use the options rw,log,noatime to enable journaling.

Final steps (moving over the data)

These are required regardless of whether using disklabel or wedges.

We’re going to copy our important directories to the new encrypted file system:

# umount /var/shm # cp -a /home /var /usr /encfs/

We need to create a symbolic link with ln because the /usr/lib directory contains some relative links to ../../, and it expects the lib directory to be there at the root. This is a hack:

# ln -s /lib /encfs/lib

Then, we move our important directories out of the way and replace them with links to the encrypted ones:

# /rescue/mv /home /home2 # /rescue/ln -s /encfs/home /home # /rescue/mv /var /var2 # /rescue/ln -s /encfs/var /var # /rescue/mv /usr /usr2 # /rescue/ln -s /encfs/usr /usr

Finally, we need to add a line to /etc/rc.conf to tell it to mount the encrypted partition early, so that /usr and /var are available during the init process:

# echo 'critical_filesystems_local="/encfs"' >> /etc/rc.conf Disclaimer

After this process, the NetBSD installer is not aware of the encrypted partition existing during upgrades. Online upgrades must be used, rather than offline upgrades where the installer is booted from removable media. This may be done with a tool like sysupgrade.

This guide was 100% written by one human and might contain human errors.

item.title: Book list for streetfighting computer scientists
item.description:
Book list for streetfighting computer scientists

2025 edition. this is very different from most "best books for programmers" lists you'll see, with Code Complete and Clean Code and Wistful Wanking for Practical Wankers and Design Slatterns and titles like that. you'll figure all that out as you go along. these are books to read so that you can cut motherfuckers with knives. do you need to read all of these? only if you want to know the things inside, i guess.

Introductory streetfighting Stepanov, From Mathematics to Generic Programming and The Elements of Programming Gustedt, Modern C Hanson, C Interfaces and Implementations Stroustrup, The C++ Programming Language Josuttis, C++ Move Semantics, because a language feature requiring 200 pages of explication is worth studying? no, because this book justifies Rust better than any text on that language. Klabnik, Nichols, and Krycho, The Rust Programming Language

need you write in C or C++? not generally. but they are a lingua franca, implemented on most hardware you'll meet, and serve as the native API expression of all operating system that matter. rust is a pretty good language to write and read, and much less to talk about all the fucking time, so cut that shit out.

Brawling combat Dijkstra, A Discipline of Programming. the most beautiful book, page-for-page, in all of computer science. Knuth, The Art of Computer Programming, especially volumes 1 and 4B, third edition Warren, Hacker's Delight. make sure you get the second edition Stevens and Rago, Advanced Programming in the UNIX Environment, get at least the second and preferably the third edition Stevens, UNIX Network Programming, second edition Abelson + Sussman, Structure and Interpretation of Computer Programs, best cover on a CS textbook hands down, second edition Varghese, Networking Algorithmics McKusick, The Design and Implementation of the FreeBSD Operating System Kerrisk, The Linux Programming Interface Garcia + Widjaja, Communications Networks. do you even ARQ, bro? Kleinrock, Queueing Systems, especially volume 1. this is why they made you take prob/stats. Hennessy + Paterson, Computer Architecture: A Quantitative Approach. the older editions don't lock material away from you online, but are...older. Kennedy, Optimizing Compilers for Modern Architectures. if you want to actually implement compilers make sure you get Muchnik's Advanced Compiler Design and Implmentation as well CLRS, Introduction to Algorithms Samet, Metric and Multidimensional Data Structures McKenney, Is Parallel Programming Hard, And, If So, What Can You Do About It? despite its preposterous title, this book is excellent, and covers things you won't find anywhere else. If Naming Books is so Hard for You, Why Didn't You Ask For Help? Crochemere et al, Algorithms on Strings. just as french as it sounds, a true force de frappe Culler et al, Parallel Computer Architecture Ward + Halstead, Computation Structures Shriver + Smith, The Anatomy of a High-Performance Microprocessor Vazirani, Approximation Algorithms Raghaven + Motwani, Randomized Algorithms Garey and Johnson, Computers and Intractability. it's always embarrassing to realize you've promised a solution to an np-complete problem. Sipser, Introduction to the Theory of Computation. but not as embarrassing as realizing you've promised a solution to an undecidable problem. also, the pumping lemma! Galub + Van Loan, Matrix Computations. this is pretty much a straight mathematics textbook, but roaming multiethnic gangs of matrices make up many streetfights. For the advanced streetfighter Ahora + Barak, Computational Complexity Pierce, Types and Programming Languages Okasaki, Purely Functional Data Structures Van Roy + Hardidi, Concepts, Techniques, and Models of Computer Programming Barendregt, The Lambda Calculus. it is true that the λ-cube is rarely useful within the tight confines of a knifefight. after a long day of bandanas and leather gloves and switchblades, even the brawler must eventually go home to family and fire and food and F systems. in a pinch, its bedazzling yellow cover can blind opponents.

speaking of math, you might want to take a look at Axler's Linear Algebra Done Right and Knuth's Concrete Mathematics. you'll want to know your combinatorics, your prob/stats, and your linear algebra cold. calculus through diffeqs is necessary to know, but i'm a pretty hardcore nerd and yet don't find myself integrating things all that often.

now go forth and fight in the streets. i list no machine learning because i dislike machine learning. there are no quantum books because quantum is not yet useful for streetfighting (we all look forward to this situation changing). i list no SIMT/accelerator books because they're all shite. i list no infosec because infosec is a subfield of QA, fight me. there are no links because i'm a lazy, lazy man.

i've heard good things about Tim Roughgarden's algorithms books, and have them on my shelves to read soon, but cannot yet speak to them. likewise Beej's book on networking, though that looks kinda lightweight. neither he nor Stevens goes into modern fast networking using things like XDP and Io_uring.

you should of course also read Hacking the Planet with Notcurses, buying copies for your team and family.

Lutnick Pushed to Weaken Chip Rules That Overlap With His Family Business

The commerce secretary has been writing new rules that would affect Southeast Asian data centers, some of which are clients of his former firm.

In Malaysia’s lush southern peninsula, a data center known as A201 is set to open next year, packed with hundreds of millions of dollars in Nvidia’s most advanced artificial intelligence servers.

The data center plans to supply this computing power to a Chinese tech giant. The setup is legal and profitable. It will also sidestep U.S. rules that ban sales of the most advanced A.I. chips directly to Chinese firms.

The company operating the data center is a client of Cantor Fitzgerald, the financial services firm formerly led by Howard Lutnick, the commerce secretary, who handed off leadership of it to his sons. Mr. Lutnick is now writing the rules that would have a substantial effect on the data center’s business.

Mr. Lutnick has been seen as a force slowing rules that would clamp down on the sale of Nvidia chips to data centers like A201, which sit outside China but provide A.I. computing power to Chinese firms.

The Trump administration, concerned about ceding the country’s advantage in A.I., bans the sale of cutting-edge chips to China. But it has been embroiled in an internal debate for much of the past two years over how far to go in limiting chip sales to data centers in Southeast Asia. On one side of the debate are China hawks, who see the data centers as a way for Beijing to do an end run around the chip sales ban. On the other are officials, most prominently Mr. Lutnick, who are pushing against going too far in limiting the ability of U.S. companies like Nvidia to sell their products in Asia.

Recently, Mr. Lutnick has been advocating a less stringent version of those controls under consideration, which could cut back on Nvidia’s business by giving the U.S. government more oversight of chip sales to international data centers. It is the latest example of Mr. Lutnick’s soft touch on chip regulation, which has prompted criticism from lawmakers and others in the administration.

item.title: Understanding Positional Embeddings in Modern LLMs
item.description:
This article explains how LLMs encode and process token position information by covering classic and contemporary methods like RoPE. It’s essentially a comprehensive journey where we will work through the mechanisms with visual examples, a little math, and a small PyTorch implementation. And, of course, we will then also look at how modern architectures adapt or omit explicit positional encodings.

Below, you can find a preview of which positional embedding choices are used in 2026 open-weight models. We will discuss these choices later after covering the underlying mechanisms.

But why spending so much time writing/reading about this rather minor building block? LLMs keep evolving, and as I was preparing a new article on the latest LLM architecture trends this year, I realized that I never covered the positional information methods used in LLMs in any article so far. So, instead of letting the other article get out of hand, I thought it might make sense to publish this as a standalone building block for the upcoming LLM architecture and trends analysis.

Also, over the years, many readers have asked me for a tutorial on relative positional embeddings (aka RoPE) to follow up on the learned absolute embeddings used in GPT. It’s been on my TODO list for a long time, so I finally revisited my old draft and put this walkthrough together, which will cover

different positional methods in LLMs;

(finally) how RoPE works;

what methods are used by recent open LLMs.

Note that this article assumes some familiarity with basic LLM architectures and works well as a follow-up to Build a Large Language Model (From Scratch). If the concepts and computation of the attention internals, particularly query, key, and value vectors, are a little fuzzy, I recommend checking my self-attention walkthrough as a refresher:

The article is also very technical and likely too detailed for some. However, I really wanted to have this foundation out there for future articles to reference. And no worries, the next one will return to a more comfortable style.

PS: I started experimenting with Substack’s new “perks” system. As a thank-you to supporters, I’ve added image exports and metadata from the architecture gallery for you to use in your own analyses.

PPS: If you are already familiar with how position embeddings work, feel free to fast-forward to Section 6, Positional choices in modern architectures.

Note that this article may be best read in a web browser than an email client. I recommend checking out the web view here, which also has a navigation bar on the left side.

1. Where position information enters an LLM

Let’s start with the overall architecture. A tokenizer encodes the input text into token IDs. Next, the input token embedding layer of an LLM maps each of these IDs to a vector of numbers. We usually refer to these entries in that vector as “features” (similar to classic ML). The transformer blocks inside the LLM then modify these vectors using attention and feedforward layers. Lastly, the model’s output layer produces logit scores (converted into probabilities) for the next token.

The following shows this path in GPT-2 (a relatively classic LLM) and MiniMax-M3 (a more recent LLM released this year; a placeholder for most other recent LLMs). As we can see, the architectures are not too different from each other, but before we get to the positional information parts, let’s focus on the orange blocks for now (the token embedding layers) and the transformer blocks above them; the other architecture differences aren’t needed for this explanation.

A token embedding layer, shown in the figure above, maps each token ID to a vector. Position information is then added afterward. Concretely, and as we will discuss in more detail later, GPT-2 adds a position vector to each token embedding before the modified embedding enters the first transformer block. On the other hand, MiniMax-M3 adds the positional information in each transformer block using a method called RoPE inside attention.

We will talk about these methods in more detail later, but first, let’s start with the big picture information explaining why explicit positional information is added or needed.

1.1 Why add positional information?

Consider the following two input sentences as a simple example:

“The red fox jumps over the gray fox.”

“The gray fox jumps over the red fox.”

Changing the word order changes which fox does the jumping, as illustrated in the following figure.

For the examples in this article, we will treat each word as one token for simplicity. (As you know, real tokenizers can split words into smaller subword tokens.) The first sentence then has eight token positions, from 0 through 7.

# Assume the following small vocabulary. # Real vocabularies typically have 50k to 200k entries vocab = { "The": 0, "red": 1, "fox": 2, "jumps": 3, "gray": 4, "over": 5, "the": 6, }

(If you are interested in how vocabularies are built, check out my tokenizer materials on GitHub.)

Note that “fox”, which appears twice in the input sentence, gets the same token ID 2 in both cases. And since they both have the same token ID, irrespective of the position in the input sentence, they would get the same embedding vector from the embedding layer.

Now, let’s consider a regular self-attention mechanism with no positional encoding (and no causal mask), where every input token can attend to every other token in the input. In this scenario, swapping any two words, like “red” and “gray”, would still result in the same embeddings and attention scores between each token pair.

GPT-style models do use a causal (autoregressive) mask, which restricts each token to itself and earlier tokens. Interestingly, this causal mask gives the computation some implicit order information. In our example, “jumps” can attend to “red” in the first sentence and “gray” in the second. So, a causal LLM can theoretically already distinguish these sentences even without explicit positional embeddings. (We will return to this idea later when discussing the “NoPE” concept.)

Nonetheless, GPT-2 and most newer LLMs include explicit positional information because it gives attention a direct signal about positions. That’s because even though the causal mask determines which tokens are accessible and provides implicit order information, it doesn’t distinguish a separation of one position from a separation of ten, for example. So, explicit positional methods are still useful (or even essential), since they supply that information.

If this all sounded confusing, don’t worry, it was more meant as an overview, and we will step through these concepts a bit more slowly in the remaining article.

2. Adding a position vector to each token embedding

We briefly talked about implicit positional information through causal attention masks (and we will revisit this again in more detail later). However, we now switch gears and talk about the explicit ways to add positional information.

The perhaps simplest and most direct (but not “cheapest”) approach is to give each sequence position its own vector. We add that vector to the token embedding, so the resulting, modified embedding vector is then passed to the first transformer block. This exact procedure is discussed in the following subsections.

2.1 Learned absolute position embeddings in GPT-2

To illustrate the use of an explicit, learned positional vector to the input embeddings, let’s consider GPT-2 as a concrete example. GPT-2 learns a table of position vectors during training. The following figure illustrates where these vectors are used in the architecture, that is, immediately after the token embedding lookup and before the first transformer block.

The positional embedding layer depicted in the figure above follows the same implementation as the token embedding layer, i.e., they have exactly the same output dimensions so that the resulting input vectors can be added to each other. The code below shows that with an excerpt of a GPT-2 code implementation:

class GPTModel(nn.Module): def __init__(self, cfg): super().__init__() self.tok_emb = nn.Embedding(cfg["vocab_size"], cfg["emb_dim"]) self.pos_emb = nn.Embedding(cfg["context_length"], cfg["emb_dim"]) self.drop_emb = nn.Dropout(cfg["drop_rate"]) self.trf_blocks = nn.Sequential( *[TransformerBlock(cfg) for _ in range(cfg["n_layers"])]) self.final_norm = LayerNorm(cfg["emb_dim"]) self.out_head = nn.Linear( cfg["emb_dim"], cfg["vocab_size"], bias=False ) def forward(self, in_idx): batch_size, seq_len = in_idx.shape tok_embeds = self.tok_emb(in_idx) pos_embeds = self.pos_emb(torch.arange(seq_len, device=in_idx.device)) x = tok_embeds + pos_embeds # Shape [batch_size, num_tokens, emb_size] x = self.drop_emb(x) x = self.trf_blocks(x) x = self.final_norm(x) logits = self.out_head(x) return logits

And in mathematical terms, we can write it as follows. Let m be a position index and xm the token ID at that position. The input to the first block is

Here,

Etoken is the embedding layer,

Pm is the position info vector selected by m,

and hm is the resulting summed embedding and position vector.

The two vectors have the same width, so we add their entries element-wise. Figure 6 below shows this visually with a small numerical example.

In the figure above, at position 0, adding the token embedding [1, 1, 1] to the position embedding [1.1, 1.2, 1.3] gives [2.1, 2.2, 2.3]. By the way, the values in the figure are chosen to keep the illustration simple; in a real example, both embedding layers (tables) are initialized with small random values and learned during training.

So, what we covered in this section is a so-called absolute positional method because the positional embedding Pm depends on the token’s own position m. In the previous example sentence, the two “fox” tokens have initially the same token embeddings, but because we are adding different positional vectors P2 and P7, they have different values before they enter the first transformer block. And consequently, the query, key, and value vectors inside the attention mechanisms then also receive representations that already include position information.

Note that the original GPT-2 implementation has 1,024 learned position vectors. This means it only works with inputs with 1024 or fewer tokens. If we want to extend the context window, we would have to extend this embedding table. And since the embedding table (layer) is updated like any other layer during training, the context length would have to be decided before the training starts.

Extending the context would be very expensive since the table can become very large. For example, in the case of GPT-2 Medium, the positional embedding layer weights only make up 0.30% of the total weights at 1,024 positions. However, if we increased the context length to a nowadays common 100k range, they would make up >22% of the total model weights, which would be very uneconomic.

2.2 Fixed sinusoidal position encodings in the original transformer

The original “Attention Is All You Need” transformer from 2017, which predates GPT, uses the same addition mechanism, but computes its position vectors with fixed sine and cosine functions. Figure 7 below shows this addition before both the encoder and decoder stacks. The encoder processes the input sequence, and the decoder generates the output sequence. (The reason why it’s introduced here is that the sine and cosine functions will become relevant again later when discussing RoPE.)

The original transformer also scales its token embeddings by √(dmodel) before adding the position vectors, where dmodel is the embedding width.

So, while GPT-2 in the previous section had the formula

the formula used in the original transformer (depicted in Figure 7) is:

This scaling by √(dmodel) is a minor technical detail, but for those who are curious, the motivation behind this scaling factor is not explained in the transformer paper, but as I discussed with colleagues on a Twitter thread many years ago, it’s likely to put the token embeddings and sinusoidal positional encodings on comparable numerical scales at initialization, so the position vectors don’t dominate the sum when we add them.

In the GPT-2 case, this scaling wasn’t necessary because the original GPT-2 code initialized the token embeddings to have an initial standard deviation of 0.02 and the position embeddings to have an initial standard deviation of 0.01 so that they were already roughly on the same scale.

Now, the more interesting point is how the position embeddings Pm are computed.

Concretely, each position vector has the following entries:

As before, m denotes the position. The index i indexes a pair of features within the vector.

Here, a feature is one number in the position vector. For example, let’s assume we have a small vector with 8 values (dmodel = 8) that has entries numbered 0 through 7. (In the original paper this was 512 for the small model and 1024 for the bigger model, instead of 8, but that would be hard to visualize.) We group these into four pairs so that i goes from 0 through 3.

Here, the indices 2i and 2i + 1 select the two entries corresponding to pair i.

As shown in the equation earlier, the angle at position m, which is then fed into the sine or cosine functions to obtain Pm, 2i or Pm, 2i + 1, respectively, is computed as follows:

Figure 10 shows this calculation for all four pairs of our 8-feature example at position m = 2.

For an eight-feature embedding, the four frequencies are 1, 0.1, 0.01, and 0.001 radians per position. At position 2, the first pair in row 1 is (sin 2, cos 2) ≈ (0.909, −0.416).

The second pair, in row 2, changes more slowly, giving (sin 0.2, cos 0.2) ≈ (0.199, 0.980).

The figure below visualizes the sine and cosine calculations for different pairs, which are then collected in a position vector.

In short, this method is a (more complicated) alternative to obtaining positional embedding vectors compared to the GPT-2 method discussed earlier.

Similar to the GPT-2 embeddings, these are also absolute embeddings because each vector is computed from its own position. However, in contrast to the GPT-2 approach, the sine and cosine functions stay fixed during training. (Also, they can be extended and evaluated beyond the training positions, like beyond the context length of 1024, although that alone doesn’t guarantee that the model will perform well there, because it hasn’t seen those during training.)

To summarize, Figure 12 below compares the two ways of obtaining a position vector we discussed so far.

This sinusoidal method may look like an overly complicated way to obtain positional embeddings, however, understanding it will be useful when talking about RoPE in the next section.

Also, there is some rationale behind it. The authors chose sine and cosine because they make the shifting by a certain offset gives a certain deterministic difference. For example, the difference between position 2 to 5 and the difference between 102 to 105 is both 3, which then results in the same rotation.

According to the Attention Is All You Need paper:

“...easily learn to attend by relative positions, since for any fixed offset k, PEpos + k can be represented as a linear function of PEpos.”

Or in less technical terms, the authors hypothesized that this property would make it easier for attention to learn relationships such as “three tokens earlier.”

Figure 13 below illustrates this for one sine/cosine pair. A rotation is a linear transformation, and both three-position shifts use the same rotation.

3. Encoding relative position with RoPE

So, the sinusoidal method above is still considered an absolute positional encoding because the vector added to each token embedding represents that token’s position counted from the start of the sequence.

As shown in the previous figure, for example, tokens at positions 2 and 5 receive the position vectors P2 and P5. If we move those tokens to positions 102 and 105, they’re still three positions apart. But each token gets a different position vector because its absolute position m has changed.

So their attention score can change even when the token embeddings stay the same. The sinusoidal structure still gives the model a way to learn relative relationships.

Anyways, RoPE, which we will discuss below, builds this relative relationship directly into the attention calculation. RoPE, which Su et al. introduced in the 2021 RoFormer paper, stands for Rotary Position Embedding and is considered a relative position method.

3.1 Moving the rotation inside attention in RoPE

In attention, each token’s current representation is projected into a query, a key, and a value vector. Query-key dot products determine attention scores. After masking and softmax, the resulting weights determine how the value vectors are mixed. For a refresher, see my Understanding and Coding Self-Attention, Multi-Head Attention, Causal-Attention, and Cross-Attention in LLMs article:

RoPE uses the token’s position to rotate its query and key vectors before their dot product. The value vectors bypass this rotation. Figure 14 below shows an overview of where RoPE is applied in a relatively recent MiniMax-M3, where QK-Norm normalizes queries and keys before RoPE.

As shown in the figure above, the LLM architecture has no explicit position vector added alongside the initial token embedding. Its explicit position signal is injected inside attention instead.

Side note: MiniMax-M3 rotates only part of each query and key head, a variation known as “partial RoPE” that we will cover later in Section 6.1. But to understand the basic RoPE operation first, let’s walk through the method step by step using a small example.

3.2 From token representations to feature pairs in RoPE

Attention usually divides its query, key, and value features into multiple heads, which are processed in parallel. Hence, the full mechanism is usually called Multi-head Attention (note that Grouped Query Attention also uses multiple heads). Here, each attention head computes its own attention scores and weighted sums. RoPE then acts on pairs of numbers within each query and key head.

To make this concrete, Figure 12 below follows a token representation through the learned query and key projections, which are computed via the weight matrices WQ and WK. In this toy example, each projection produces 16 features, which are reshaped into two heads with eight features each. In the figure below, every small cell contains one scalar feature, meaning one numerical entry in a vector (the numbers are not shown due to space reasons).

For the first eight-feature head, [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8], we pair each feature in the first half with the corresponding feature in the second half. This gives (1, 5), (2, 6), (3, 7), and (4, 8). This split-half convention is used in LLM implementations, including my Qwen3 implementation. (We will compare it with the original, alternative adjacent-feature pairing method later after implementing the basic operation.)

Each pair gets a rotation angle determined by the token position m and that pair’s frequency θi. The corresponding query and key pairs use the same frequency. Figure 16 below shows how we rotate the pairs, put the updated features back in their original locations, and compute the query-key dot product.

The next section will walk through the figure(s) a bit more slowly.

3.3 Rotating one pair in RoPE

For the following example, we’ll use the same two positions as before. The query comes from “the” at position m = 5, and the key comes from the first “fox” at position n = 2. Since, in this example, the key comes before the query, the causal mask allows the query to attend to it.

To illustrate the effect that the position has, and keeping everything fixed, let’s assume we start both pairs from the same two values, (1, 5).

Furthermore, for this example, let’s use θ = 20° per token position (π/9 radians per position). At position 2, we rotate the key’s arrow counterclockwise by 2 × 20° = 40°. At position 5, we rotate the query’s arrow by 5 × 20° = 100°.

To illustrate what’s happening in the figure above, for example, plugging cos 40° ≈ 0.766 and sin 40° ≈ 0.643 into the rotation from Figure 16 gives the new key coordinates:

Then, changing 40° to 100°, using the same equation as above, the rotated query pair becomes q′ ≈ (−5.098, 0.117). But the important point is that both arrows still have length √26. Only the rotation changes but the vectors keep the same lengths after the transformation.

So, for a query pair (a, b) at position m, the two operations here are.

For the key pair at position n, we use the same equations with nθ.

(Section 4 later shows how RoPE calculates the angular frequency for each feature pair.)

To close this section, for those more comfortable reading code, everything about RoPE illustrated so far can be written in code, as follows:

import torch query_head = torch.tensor([1., 2., 3., 4., 5., 6., 7., 8.]) key_head = query_head.clone() # Split-half pairing gives (1, 5), (2, 6), (3, 7), and (4, 8). query_pairs = torch.stack(query_head.chunk(2), dim=-1) key_pairs = torch.stack(key_head.chunk(2), dim=-1) # Take the first feature pair from each head. q = query_pairs[0] k = key_pairs[0] m = 5 # Query position (in our example, "the") n = 2 # Key position (in our example, the first "fox") theta = torch.deg2rad(torch.tensor(20.0)) # Radians per token position def rotate_pair(pair, angle): a, b = pair c, s = torch.cos(angle), torch.sin(angle) return torch.stack((a * c - b * s, a * s + b * c)) k_rot = rotate_pair(k, n * theta) # 2 × 20° = 40° q_rot = rotate_pair(q, m * theta) # 5 × 20° = 100° print(f"Original key: ({k[0]:g}, {k[1]:g})") print(f"Original query: ({q[0]:g}, {q[1]:g})") print(f"Rotated key: ({k_rot[0]:.3f}, {k_rot[1]:.3f})") print(f"Rotated query: ({q_rot[0]:.3f}, {q_rot[1]:.3f})")

The resulting values are:

Original key: (1, 5) Original query: (1, 5) Rotated key: (-2.448, 4.473) Rotated query: (-5.098, 0.117)

If we rotate all 4 pairs in the 8-feature query (and key) vector(s), we get the vectors below. (We’ll come back to how we go from rotating one pair to rotating all of them later.)

Original key: (1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8) Original query: (1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8) Rotated key: (-2.448, 1.577, 2.951, 3.994, 4.473, 6.125, 7.021, 8.003) Rotated query: (-5.098, 0.928, 2.877, 3.986, 0.117, 6.256, 7.051, 8.007) 3.4 How the relative offset changes the attention score in RoPE

Note that, as shown above, the query and key heads have eight features each, which we previously grouped into 4 pairs with two elements each, like (1, 5), and (2, 6), and so on. For simplicity here we’ll follow just the first pair in each head, (1, 5), formed by taking the entries at indices 0 and 4:

Original key: (1, 5) Original query: (1, 5) Rotated key: (-2.448, 4.473) Rotated query: (-5.098, 0.117)

As shown above, in our example, those entries have values (1, 5) in both heads before the rotation.

Also, as in the code above, let’s use the notation q =(q1, q2) and k =(k1, k2) for these two pairs. To compute their dot product, using the standard dot product formula, we multiply corresponding coordinates and add the products:

Before rotation, the pairs have a dot product of 1 × 1 + 5 × 5 = 26. Using the rounded coordinates from the previous Figure 18 gives the contribution from the first pair after rotation:

We can see why by writing the dot product in terms of the lengths of the two vectors (arrows in Figure 18) and the angle ϕ between them.

In both cases, the vector length is √26. The query (position 5) is rotated by 100° and the key (position 2) is rotated by 40°. The vectors (arrows) start from the same direction, so they end up being 60° apart after rotation. Their exact dot product is 26 × cos(60°) = 13.

Now let’s see what happens if we move just the key from position 2 to position 3, but we keep its starting coordinates (1, 5) fixed. The key’s rotation changes now from 2 × 20° = 40° to 3 × 20° = 60°. The query still rotates by 100°, so the angle between the arrows shrinks to 40° and the dot product changes from 13 to 26 × cos(40°) ≈ 19.92. So, moving the key one position closer changed the dot product even though we started with the same feature values.

Why do these dot products matter? In attention, we sum the contributions from all feature pairs to get the query-key dot products. RoPE can change those dot products and thus the weights that softmax assigns to the value vectors.

In the attention equation above, Q′ and K′ are matrices that contain the rotated queries q′ and keys k′ for one head, V contains the values, and d is the head dimension.

3.5 Why shifting both positions preserves the attention score in RoPE

Now that we illustrated the computation of the dot products, which is at the core of the attention mechanism, let’s return to positions m = 5 and n = 2. If we shift both positions to the right by three positions, we get m = 8 and n = 5. Each rotation gains 60° (the query goes from 100° to 160°, and the key goes from 40° to 100°), however, the angle between the vectors stays the same. The dot product for this feature pair is still 13.

The key is that the difference between the rotation angles is

If we keep the original query and key vectors fixed and shift both token positions by the same amount, RoPE adds the same rotation to both vectors. The angle between them stays the same, so their dot product stays the same. Note that Figure 20 below uses smaller angles than the actual example (20° per position) to keep the picture readable.

The examples above and Figure 20 illustrate the main idea behind RoPE. We use each token’s position to rotate the corresponding query and key in the attention module. In the query-key dot product, what matters is how much one vector rotates relative to the other. For each feature pair, this difference in rotation depends only on the offset between the two tokens.

To illustrate this in the big picture context, in Figure 21, each row collects the scores for one query. If we consider row 5, the query for “the”, and column 2, the key for “fox”, the attention score between those two is computed as the dot product between the two rotated versions of the query and key vector.

What’s the point, again? Let’s once more consider “The red fox jumps over the gray fox.” If we add 100 tokens (e.g., think system prompt) before the sentence, the first “fox” and the second “the” move from positions 2 and 5 to 102 and 105. However, a prefix of any length shifts both positions equally, so they still stay exactly three positions apart. This means, each vector (arrow) gains the exact same additional rotation, which preserves the angle between them and their dot product (assuming we hold the unrotated query and key vectors fixed; in a real model, a new prefix of 100 tokens can change those vectors by changing what the tokens attend to).

Figure 22 tracks this comparison in the attention score matrix. The right panel shows the rows and columns for the sentence after we add the prefix. In our toy example, the first pair still contributes 13 to the dot product.

As you may recall, in the original transformer’s sinusoidal encoding, a fixed offset also corresponds to a fixed rotation within each sine/cosine pair. But that shared rotation applies only to the position vectors (added to the input vector) instead of the key and query vectors inside the attention mechanism.

4. Computing rotation frequencies in RoPE?

A full attention head uses multiple frequencies so that some feature pairs change more drastically (”quickly” in RoPE terms) with position and others change more gradually (”slowly” in RoPE terms). This serves the same purpose as the multiple frequencies in the original transformer’s sinusoidal encodings.

However, instead of us assigning these manually, for a head with d features, standard full RoPE computes one frequency for each of its d/2 pairs as follows:

Here,

d is the head dimension (it has to be even so that all features can be arranged in pairs).

i is the index of the pair; it ranges from 0 to d/2−1.

b is a chosen base value (hyperparameter) that determines the spacing of the frequencies.

θi is pair i‘s frequency in radians per token position.

The original RoFormer paper uses b = 10,000, borrowing the original transformer’s frequency formula with head dimension d in place of embedding width dmodel.

For example, with head dimension d = 8 and base b = 10,000, we get frequencies [1, 0.1, 0.01, 0.001] radians per position.
